extraction_notes.note: The two \item substitutions in the proof of the sum-of-updates lemma are author labels (step rule 1), but the first is a lone 'Let' sentence (step rule 4); kept them as two steps and left the \item token in their statements to satisfy both checks.

The auxiliary moments m', v', the update u_t, U_t and tilde v are introduced inside the prose proof of Theorem 1 (so they are steps, step rule 4) but are used by lemma statements in A.3-A.15; the term edges go from the numbered equation nodes that define them.

The proof environment of Theorem 2 sits under a subsection titled 'Proof of Theorem', with no syntactic link; its proves edge is set from that title. The appendix proof-dependency diagram is omitted from the source.
Numbered display named in the text as the weighted Young's inequality: retyped from equation to theorem (external, standard).
The proof of Theorem 1 has no proof environment; taken as the whole subsection A.2 'Detailed Proof', including the closing asymptotic analysis of the six terms.
claim or remark: the bf16 relative-error bound is derived from the preceding construction rather than proved separately; it motivates Assumption 1.
Experimental setups, hyperparameters and figure discussions (Section 4 Experiments, Appendix C) are not extracted, except the Rosenbrock objective definition.

nodes.statement: Scalars are denoted by lowercase letters ($x, \ldots$), vectors by bold lowercase ($\xb, \ldots$), and matrices by bold uppercase ($\Xb, \ldots$).
nodes.name: Notation conventions for scalars, vectors and matrices

nodes.statement: The $i$-th entry of $\xb$ is $x_i$, and the $(i,j)$-th entry of $\Xb$ is $X_{ij}$.
nodes.name: Entry notation

nodes.statement: The $\ell_2$ norm of $\xb$ is $\|\xb\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_i x_i^2}$, the Frobenius norm of $\Xb$ is $\|\Xb\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i,j} X_{ij}^2}$, and the nuclear norm of $\Xb$ is $\|\Xb\|_* = \sum_i \sigma_i(\Xb)$, where $\sigma_i(\Xb)$ denotes the $i$-th singular value.
nodes.name: Vector l2, Frobenius and nuclear norms
nodes.statement_short: Defines the l2 norm, the Frobenius norm and the nuclear norm (sum of singular values).

nodes.statement: For $d \in \NN^+$, let $[d] = \{1,2,\ldots,d\}$.
nodes.name: Index set [d]

nodes.statement: For real sequences $\{a_t\}$ and $\{b_t\}$, we write $a_t = O(b_t)$ if there exist constants $C,N>0$ such that $a_t \le Cb_t$ for all $t \ge N$; $a_t = \Omega(b_t)$ if $b_t = O(a_t)$; $a_t = \Theta(b_t)$ if both $a_t = O(b_t)$ and $a_t = \Omega(b_t)$; and we use $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ and $\tilde{\Omega}(\cdot)$ to suppress logarithmic factors.
nodes.name: Asymptotic notation O, Omega, Theta
nodes.statement_short: Standard big-O, big-Omega, big-Theta notation; tilde versions hide log factors.

nodes.statement: The quantization operator is $\cQ(\cdot)$, with $x^Q$ denoting the quantized version of $x$.
nodes.name: Quantization operator notation

nodes.statement: Let $\cQ:\RR \to \RR$ be a scalar quantization operator applied elementwise to vectors and matrices.
nodes.name: Scalar quantization operator
differentia: applied elementwise to vectors and matrices

nodes.statement: The fp32 format uses $1$ sign bit, $8$ exponent bits, and $23$ mantissa bits (total $32$ bits) \citep{IEEE754}, while bf16 keeps the same sign and exponent layout but truncates the mantissa to $7$ bits \citep{wang2019bfloat16}.
nodes.name: fp32 and bf16 formats

nodes.statement: Thus, FP32 can be written as \[ x_{\text{fp32}} = (-1)^{S}\times 2^{E-127}\times (1.M_{0:22}), \] where $S$ is the sign bit, $E$ the exponent, and $M_{0:22}$ the mantissa bits.
nodes.name: FP32 representation
nodes.statement_short: An fp32 number is (-1)^S 2^{E-127} (1.M) with sign bit S, exponent E and 23 mantissa bits.

nodes.statement: The BF16 number becomes \[ x_{\text{bf16}} = (-1)^{S}\times 2^{E-127}\times \big(1.M_{0:6} + C \cdot 2^{-7}\big), \] where $C\in\{0,1\}$ is a carry bit from rounding.
nodes.name: BF16 quantized representation
nodes.statement_short: The bf16 quantization keeps 7 mantissa bits plus a rounding carry bit C.

nodes.statement: The above construction implies that the quantization error satisfies \[ |x_{\text{bf16}} - x_{\text{fp32}}| = \big|C \cdot 2^{-7} - 0.M_{7:22}\cdot 2^{-7}\big| \cdot 2^{E-127} \;\le\; 2^{-7} \cdot 2^{E-127} \;\le\; q |x_{\text{fp32}}|, \] where $q=\Theta(2^{-M})$ and $M$ is the mantissa length of the target format (here $M=7$ for bf16).
nodes.name: Relative error bound of floating-point quantization
assumptions: where $q=\Theta(2^{-M})$ and $M$ is the mantissa length of the target format
nodes.statement_short: Truncating fp32 to bf16 gives a relative error at most q|x| with q = Theta(2^{-M}).

nodes.statement: More generally, we assume the absence of underflow and overflow, so that the sign and exponent remain unchanged after quantization.
nodes.name: No underflow or overflow

nodes.statement: Let $\cQ:\RR \to \RR$ be a scalar quantization operator applied elementwise. Then, for any $x\in\RR$, the quantization error is relatively bounded: \[ |x^Q - x| \le q |x|, \] where $q=\Theta(2^{-M})$, and $M$ is the mantissa length of the target floating-point format.
nodes.name: Quantization Error
nodes.statement_short: Elementwise quantization has relative error |x^Q - x| <= q|x| with q = Theta(2^{-M}).
nodes.label: assump:qe

nodes.statement: Formally, the goal is to minimize the loss: \begin{align} \min_{\Wb \in \RR^{m\times n}} F(\Wb) = \EE_{\bxi}[f(\Wb; \bxi)], \end{align} where $\Wb$ denotes the model parameters, $\bxi$ is a random variable representing the data, and $f(\Wb;\bxi)$ is the sample loss.
nodes.name: Stochastic optimization problem
nodes.statement_short: Minimize F(W) = E_xi[f(W; xi)] over weight matrices W.

nodes.statement: \min_{\Wb \in \RR^{m\times n}} F(\Wb) = \EE_{\bxi}[f(\Wb; \bxi)],
nodes.name: Expected loss minimization
nodes.label: eq:opt

nodes.statement: We denote $F^* = \inf_{\Wb} F(\Wb) > -\infty$ as the optimal objective value.
nodes.name: Optimal objective value

nodes.statement: The key steps are: \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*] \item The master maintains full-precision weights $\Wb_t$ but transmits their quantized version $\Wb_t^Q$ to workers. \item Workers perform forward and backward passes with $\Wb_t^Q$, compute gradients $\nabla f(\Wb_t^Q; \bxi)$, quantize them, and send quantized gradients back. \item The master dequantizes gradients, updates quantized optimizer states (e.g., momentum, second moment), and applies the optimizer update. Updated states are re-quantized for storage.
nodes.name: Low-precision training framework
nodes.statement_short: Master keeps full-precision weights, workers compute gradients on quantized weights; master updates quantized optimizer states.

nodes.statement: We denote the relative errors $q$ of different components after applying $\cQ$ as \[ q_W \quad \text{(weights)}, \qquad q_G \quad \text{(gradients)}, \qquad q_M \quad \text{(first moment)}, \qquad q_V \quad \text{(second moment)}. \]
nodes.name: Component-wise relative errors

nodes.statement: Formally, for any quantized quantity $\Xb_t$ (e.g., $\Wb_t$, $\Gb_t$, $\Mb_t$, $\Vb_t$) at iteration $t$, its relative quantization error is defined as the smallest constant $q \ge 0$ such that \[ \vert [\Xb_t^Q]_{ij} - [\Xb_t]_{ij} \vert \le q_X \vert [\Xb_t]_{ij}\vert, \qquad \forall t \in {0, \dots, T-1}. \]
nodes.name: Relative quantization error of a quantity
nodes.statement_short: The relative quantization error of X_t is the smallest q with |[X_t^Q]_ij - [X_t]_ij| <= q|[X_t]_ij| for all t.

nodes.statement: In particular, we have \begin{align*} q_W &:= \inf\big\{q \ge 0 : |[\Wb_t^Q]_{ij} - [\Wb_t]_{ij}| \le q |[\Wb_t]_{ij}|, \forall t\big\},\\ q_G &:= \inf\big\{q \ge 0 : |[\Gb_t^Q]_{ij} - [\Gb_t]_{ij}| \le q |[\Gb_t]_{ij}|, \forall t\big\},\\ q_M &:= \inf\big\{q \ge 0 : |[\Mb_t^Q]_{ij} - [\Mb_t]_{ij}| \le q |[\Mb_t]_{ij}|, \forall t\big\},\\ q_V &:= \inf\big\{q \ge 0 : |[\Vb_t^Q]_{ij} - [\Vb_t]_{ij}| \le q |[\Vb_t]]_{ij}|, \forall t\big\}. \end{align*}
nodes.name: Relative errors q_W, q_G, q_M, q_V as infima
nodes.statement_short: q_W, q_G, q_M, q_V are the smallest constants bounding the elementwise relative error of weights, gradients, first and second moments.

nodes.statement: \caption{Analytical Adaptive Method Quantization Training Framework} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \State \textbf{Input 1}: Algorithm $\cA\in \{\mathrm{Adam},\mathrm{Muon} \}$ and its parameters set $\bTheta \in \{\{ \beta_1,\beta_2,\epsilon \},\{\beta \} \}$, initial weights $\Wb_0$, learning rate schedule $\{\eta_t\}$, batch size $B$, quantization operator $\cQ$ \For{$t = 0, \ldots, T-1$} \State Sample batch $\{\bxi_{t,i}\}_{i=1}^B$ uniformly \Comment{$B$ workers} \State $\Gb_t = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B \nabla^Q f(\Wb_t^Q; \bxi_{t,i})$ \Comment{Master receives $B$ quantized gradients} \State $\Wb_{t+1} = \cA(\Wb_t, \Gb_t, \bTheta, t)$ \Comment{Update by Adam or Muon} \EndFor \end{algorithmic}
nodes.name: Analytical Adaptive Method Quantization Training Framework
input: \textbf{Input 1}: Algorithm $\cA\in \{\mathrm{Adam},\mathrm{Muon} \}$ and its parameters set $\bTheta \in \{\{ \beta_1,\beta_2,\epsilon \},\{\beta \} \}$, initial weights $\Wb_0$, learning rate schedule $\{\eta_t\}$, batch size $B$, quantization operator $\cQ$
nodes.statement_short: Training loop: sample a batch, average quantized gradients at quantized weights, update with Adam or Muon.
nodes.label: alg:framework

nodes.statement: \caption{Adam$(\Wb_t, \Gb_t, \bTheta, t)$} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \State $\{\beta_1, \beta_2, \epsilon\} \leftarrow \bTheta$ \State $\Mb_t \leftarrow \beta_1 \Mb_{t-1}^Q + \Gb_t$ if $t>0$ else $\Mb_0 = \Gb_0$ \State $\Vb_t \leftarrow \beta_2 \Vb_{t-1}^Q + \Gb_t^2$ if $t>0$ else $\Vb_0 = \Gb_0^2$ \State \Return $\Wb_t - \eta_t \Mb_t/\sqrt{{\Vb_t}+ \epsilon\mathbf{1}}$ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.name: Adam
nodes.statement_short: Adam step with quantized stored moments: M_t = beta1 M_{t-1}^Q + G_t, V_t = beta2 V_{t-1}^Q + G_t^2, W - eta M/sqrt(V+eps).
nodes.label: alg:adam

nodes.statement: \caption{Muon$(\Wb_t, \Gb_t, \bTheta, t)$} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \State $\{\beta \} \leftarrow \bTheta$ \State $\Mb_t = \beta \Mb_{t-1}^Q + (1-\beta)\Gb_t$ if $t>0$ else $\Mb_0 = \Gb_0$ \State $(\Ub_t, \Sbb_t, \Vb_t) = \mathrm{SVD}(\Mb_t)$ \State \Return $\Wb_t - \eta_t \Ub_t\Vb_t^{\top}$ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.name: Muon
nodes.statement_short: Muon step: momentum with quantized state, SVD of the momentum, update W - eta U V^T.
nodes.label: alg:muon

The stochastic gradient $
abla f(\Wb; xi)$ is an unbiased estimator of the true gradient $
abla F(\Wb)$, i.e., $\EE[
abla f(\Wb; xi)] = 
abla F(\Wb)$.
nodes.name: Unbiased Stochastic Gradient
nodes.label: assump:grad_unbiased

nodes.statement:
The stochastic gradient $
abla f(\Wb; xi)$ satisfies the following bounds depending on the algorithm:  egin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item { f Adam}: The stochastic gradient is $\ell_\infty$ uniformly almost surely bounded, i.e., there exists a constant $R > \sqrt{\epsilon}$ (where $\epsilon > 0$ is the stability constant used to simplify the final bounds) such that  egin{align*} \|
abla f(\Wb; xi)\|_\infty = \max_{i,j} |[
abla f(\Wb; xi)]_{ij}| \le R - \sqrt{\epsilon}, \quad 	ext{a.s.}. \end{align*} \item { f Muon}: The stochastic gradient has bounded variance, i.e., there exists a constant $\sigma > 0$ such that  egin{align*} \EE[\|
abla f(\Wb; xi) - 
abla F(\Wb)\|_F^2] \le \sigma^2. \end{align*} \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Stochastic Gradient Bounds
nodes.statement_short: Adam: stochastic gradients bounded in l_inf by R - sqrt(eps) a.s.; Muon: gradient variance at most sigma^2.
nodes.label: assump:grad_bounds

nodes.statement: The objective function $F:\RR^{m\times n}\to\RR$ is $L$-smooth, i.e., for any $\Xb, \Yb \in \RR^{m\times n}$, we have \begin{align*} \|\nabla F(\Xb) - \nabla F(\Yb)\|_F \;\le\; L \|\Xb - \Yb\|_F. \end{align*}
nodes.name: Smoothness
nodes.label: assump:smooth

nodes.statement:
We remark that a more general $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness condition~\citep{zhang2020why}, which has been adopted in recent analyses of Adam~\citep{li2023convergence,wang2024provable,hong2024convergence}, allows the smoothness constant to depend on the gradient norm: $\|
abla F(\Xb) - 
abla F(\Yb)\|_F \le (L_0 + L_1 \|
abla F(\Yb)\|_F) \|\Xb - \Yb\|_F$.
nodes.name: (L0,L1)-smoothness
nodes.statement_short: Generalized smoothness whose constant L0 + L1 ||grad F|| grows with the gradient norm.

nodes.statement: The initial parameter matrix $\Wb_0$ and its gradient are bounded in Frobenius norm, i.e., $\|\Wb_0\|_F \le D,\ \|\nabla F(\Wb_0)\|_F \le G$, for some constants $D,G > 0$.
nodes.name: Bounded Initialization
nodes.label: assump:bound_init

nodes.name: Convergence of Quantized Adam

nodes.statement_short: Quantized Adam's weighted-random-iterate squared gradient norm is bounded by quantization-dependent terms; with q_G,q_M=O(1/T), q_W,q_V=O(1/T^2) it converges at rate O~(T^{-1/4}).
nodes.label: thm:QAdam

nodes.statement: Our theorem further reveals a nuanced sensitivity to different types of quantization error. The required precision for the second moment ($q_V$) is stricter than for the first moment ($q_M$). This sensitivity arises because accumulated errors in the second-moment estimate $\Vb_t$ are non-linearly amplified by the update step's inverse square root. This theoretical finding provides a rigorous explanation for the empirical observation that the second moment often require higher precision than the first moment in low-bit training setups \citep{peng2023fp8,tao2024collage,fishman2025scaling}. Similarly, the stricter precision requirement for weights ($q_W = \cO(1/T^2)$) is necessary to control error accumulation over the entire training trajectory. Our analysis must account for the potential growth of weight magnitudes throughout training, which acts as an amplification factor for the relative quantization error. To guarantee convergence under this worst-case scenario of unbounded weight growth, the proof requires $q_W$ to decay rapidly to counteract this amplification. However, this strict condition is a consequence of the proof's generality. In practice, where weight norms often remain bounded, this error amplification is less severe, and the precision requirement for $q_W$ could be relaxed to $\cO(1/T)$.
nodes.name: Sensitivity of Adam to second-moment and weight quantization
nodes.statement_short: Second-moment errors are amplified by the inverse square root, so q_V and q_W need O(1/T^2) precision, likely loose in practice.

nodes.statement: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assump:qe},~\ref{assump:grad_unbiased}–\ref{assump:bound_init} hold. Consider the Quantized Muon algorithm in \ref{alg:framework} and~\ref{alg:muon} run for $T$ iterations with $\eta_t=\eta,\beta(1+q_M) < 1$, then \begin{align*} \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\EE[\| \nabla F(\Wb_t) \|_F] &\le \frac{\EE[F(\Wb_0)-F(\Wb_T)]}{\eta T} + \frac{2\beta L\eta r}{1-\beta} + \frac{6\sigma\sqrt{r}}{T(1-\beta)\sqrt{B}}+ \sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}}\frac{6\sigma\sqrt{r}}{\sqrt{B}} + \\ &\frac{L\eta r}{2} + C_{2}\cdot\bigg(q_G+ q_W + q_G T\eta + q_W T\eta + \frac{q_M\beta}{1-\beta(1+q_M)}(1+T\eta) \bigg) , \end{align*} where $C_2$ is absolute constant, $r=\min\{m,n\}$. Moreover, suppose $F(\Wb_0) - F^* \le \Delta$ for constant $\Delta > 0$, set $1-\beta = \Theta(T^{-1/2})$, $\eta = \Theta(T^{-3/4})$, and $B = 1$, if $q_G = q_W = q_M = \cO(T^{-1/2})$, then \begin{align*} \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\EE[\| \nabla F(\Wb_t) \|_F] = \cO(T^{-1/4}). \end{align*}

nodes.statement_short: Quantized Muon's average gradient norm is bounded by full-precision terms plus O(q_G + q_W + q_M terms); with q = O(T^{-1/2}) it converges at O(T^{-1/4}).
nodes.label: thm:QMuon

nodes.statement: As a sanity check, when $q_W = q_G = q_M = 0$, our result recovers the exact convergence rate $\cO(1/T^{1/4})$ of \citet{shen2025convergence} up to constant factors. More importantly, as long as the mantissa length of the floating-point format scales logarithmically with $T$, i.e., $M = \Omega(\log T)$, the quantization errors decay as $q_W=q_G=q_M=\cO(T^{-1/2})$. With appropriate choices of $\eta$ and $\beta$ (as in Theorem~\ref{thm:QMuon}), the full-precision convergence rate $\cO(T^{-1/4})$ is preserved.
nodes.name: Recovery of full-precision Muon rate
nodes.statement_short: With zero quantization error Theorem 2 recovers the O(T^{-1/4}) Muon rate; mantissa length Omega(log T) suffices.

nodes.statement: Finally, we highlight a sharp contrast with quantized Adam. Theorem~\ref{thm:QMuon} requires only relative errors on the order of $q=\cO(T^{-1/2})$, whereas Theorem~\ref{thm:QAdam} demands stricter conditions, at least $q=\cO(T^{-1})$ and in some cases $q=\cO(T^{-2})$. This theoretical distinction explains why Muon adapts more efficiently to low-precision settings than Adam, corroborating the empirical observations of \citet{liu2025muon}.
nodes.name: Muon versus Adam precision requirements
nodes.statement_short: Muon needs only q = O(T^{-1/2}) while Adam needs O(T^{-1}) or O(T^{-2}), explaining Muon's robustness.

nodes.statement: Let $\Wb \in \RR^{m\times n}$, and define $F(\Wb) = \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \Big(100\|\Wb_{j+1}-\Wb_j^2\|_F^2 + \|\mathbf{1}_{m} - \Wb_j\|_F^2\Big)$, where $\Wb_j$ denotes the $j$-th column of $\Wb$ and $\mathbf{1}_m$ is the $m$-dimensional all-ones vector.
nodes.name: Rosenbrock function
also_stated_at: We conduct synthetic experiments on the Rosenbrock function, defined as \begin{align*} F(\Wb) = \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \Big( 100\|\Wb_{j+1} - \Wb_j^2\|_F^2 + \|\mathbf{1}_m-\Wb_j\|_F^2 \Big), \end{align*} where $\Wb = [\Wb_1,\Wb_2,\dots,\Wb_d] \in \RR^{m\times n}$ is the weight matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Matrix Rosenbrock objective summing 100||W_{j+1} - W_j^2||^2 + ||1 - W_j||^2 over columns.

nodes.statement: In practice, bit-width is typically fixed (e.g., FP8 or BF16), which means convergence is guaranteed only to a neighborhood of a stationary point; understanding why moderate fixed precision suffices empirically remains an open question.
nodes.name: Why fixed moderate precision suffices
nodes.statement_short: Explain why fixed moderate precision (FP8/BF16) suffices empirically, beyond the M = Omega(log T) regime.

nodes.statement: We consider an optimization problem in a $d$-dimensional space (let $d=mn$ be the number of trainable parameters), where coordinates are indexed by $i \in [d] = \{1, 2, \ldots, d\}$.
nodes.name: Dimension d and coordinate indices

nodes.statement: Our algorithm generates a sequence of vectors $(\ub_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}}$, with the $i$-th component of $\ub_t$ denoted by $u_{t,i}$.
nodes.name: Iterate sequence u_t

nodes.statement: The objective is to find a critical point of a global function $F: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ within a stochastic framework, where we have access to a sequence of i.i.d. sample functions $(f_t)_{t \in \mathbb{N}^*}$ (e.g., the loss on a data minibatch).
nodes.name: Sample functions f_t

nodes.statement: For any differentiable function $h: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, we denote its gradient by $\nabla h$ and its $i$-th component by $\nabla_i h$.
nodes.name: Gradient notation

nodes.statement: Finally, we use a small constant $\epsilon > 0$ for numerical stability and let $\mathbb{E}_t[\cdot]$ denote the conditional expectation given the history of samples $f_1, \ldots, f_{t-1}$.
nodes.name: Stability constant and conditional expectation

nodes.statement: We use $\vec(\cdot)$ to vectorize a matrix and $\mat(\cdot)$ for the inverse operation.
nodes.name: Vectorization operators

nodes.statement: In the proof, we denote $\wb_t=\vec(\Wb_t)$, $\hat{\gb_t}=\vec(\Gb_t)$ and the dimension $d=m \cdot n$.
nodes.name: Vectorized weights and gradients

nodes.statement: The standard first moment, often expressed as $\tilde{m}_{t, i} = (1-\beta_1) \sum_{k=1}^{t}\beta_1^{t - k} \hat{g}_{k,i}$, is simply a scaled version of our definition, i.e., $\tilde{m}_{t,i} = (1 - \beta_1) m_{t,i}$.
nodes.name: Standard weighted-average first moment

nodes.statement: Furthermore, the standard Adam algorithm includes bias correction terms to counteract the zero-initialization of moments. These corrections are equivalent to using a time-dependent step size of the form: \begin{equation} \eta_{t, \text{Adam}} = \eta \cdot \frac{1 - \beta_1}{\sqrt{1 - \beta_2}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{1 - \beta_2^t}}{1 - \beta_1^t}. \end{equation}
nodes.name: Adam bias correction as step size
nodes.statement_short: Adam's bias corrections equal a time-dependent step size eta (1-beta1)/sqrt(1-beta2) sqrt(1-beta2^t)/(1-beta1^t).

nodes.statement: For analytical tractability, our analysis adopts the simplified step size $\eta_t$ from \eqref{app:eq:alpha_adam}, which omits the bias correction for the first moment ($m_{t,i}$). This simplification is motivated by several practical and theoretical considerations. First, it ensures that our step size $\eta_t$ is monotonic with respect to $t$, which is advantageous for the convergence proof. Second, for typical hyperparameter values (e.g., $\beta_1=0.9$, $\beta_2=0.999$), the omitted term $1/(1-\beta_1^t)$ converges to its limit of 1 much more rapidly than the retained term $\sqrt{1 - \beta_2^t}$. Finally, removing this term effectively implements a learning rate warm-up, a common and beneficial practice, while retaining the correction for $v_{t,i}$ prevents an undesirably large initial step size that could lead to training instability.
nodes.name: Simplified step size without first-moment bias correction
nodes.statement_short: Dropping the first-moment bias correction keeps eta_t monotone and acts as warm-up.

nodes.statement: Our theoretical framework analyzes the quantization of weighted-sum moments ($\mb_t, \vb_t$), while a practical implementation would quantize the standard weighted-average moments ($\tilde{\mb}_t, \tilde{\vb}_t$). We now prove that these two approaches are, in fact, analytically equivalent.
nodes.name: Equivalence of quantization schemes
nodes.statement_short: Quantizing weighted-sum moments is analytically equivalent to quantizing weighted-average moments.

nodes.statement: Consider two scalar sequences $\{a_k\}_{k\ge0}$ and $\{c_k\}_{k\ge0}$ evolving according to the following dynamics for $k \ge 1$, with initial conditions $a_0 = c_0 = 0$: \begin{align} a_k &= \beta(a_{k-1} + d_{k-1}) + b_k \\ c_k &= \beta(c_{k-1} + e_{k-1}) + (1-\beta)b_k \end{align} where $\beta \in (0,1)$ is a decay factor, $\{b_k\}$ is an external input sequence, and $\{d_k\}, \{e_k\}$ are perturbation sequences. These perturbations are bounded by a relative error model with factor $q \in [0,1)$: \begin{align} |d_{k-1}| \le q|a_{k-1}| \quad \text{and} \quad |e_{k-1}| \le q|c_{k-1}|. \end{align} Then, the sequence $\{c_k\}$ and the scaled sequence $\{a'_k\} \triangleq (1-\beta)a_k$ are analytically equivalent. Specifically, they follow identical recurrence relations where their respective perturbation terms satisfy identical relative error bounds with respect to their own states.
nodes.name: Equivalence of Perturbed Dynamical Systems
assumptions: $\beta \in (0,1)$ is a decay factor
These perturbations are bounded by a relative error model with factor $q \in [0,1)$

nodes.statement_short: Weighted-sum and weighted-average recursions with relative-error perturbations obey the same recurrence and relative error bounds.
nodes.label: lemma:dynamical_equivalence

nodes.name: Relative perturbation bounds
nodes.label: eq:error_bounds

nodes.statement: To prove the equivalence, we derive the recurrence relation for the scaled sequence $\{a'_k\}$ and compare its structure and error properties to that of $\{c_k\}$. \textbf{Step 1: Derive the recurrence for $\{a'_k\}$.} Starting from the definition $a'_k = (1-\beta)a_k$ and substituting the dynamics from \eqref{eq:system_a}: \begin{align*} a'_k &= (1-\beta) \left[ \beta(a_{k-1} + d_{k-1}) + b_k \right] \\ &= \beta(1-\beta)a_{k-1} + \beta(1-\beta)d_{k-1} + (1-\beta)b_k. \end{align*} Now, we replace $a_{k-1}$ with $a'_{k-1}/(1-\beta)$: \begin{align*} a'_k &= \beta(1-\beta)\left(\frac{a'_{k-1}}{1-\beta}\right) + \beta(1-\beta)d_{k-1} + (1-\beta)b_k \\ &= \beta a'_{k-1} + \beta(1-\beta)d_{k-1} + (1-\beta)b_k. \end{align*} \textbf{Step 2: Compare recurrence structures.} Let us place the recurrence relations for $\{c_k\}$ and $\{a'_k\}$ side-by-side: \begin{align*} c_k &= \beta c_{k-1} + \beta e_{k-1} + (1-\beta)b_k \\ a'_k &= \beta a'_{k-1} + \beta(1-\beta)d_{k-1} + (1-\beta)b_k. \end{align*} Both sequences share the identical structure: $X_k = \beta X_{k-1} + \text{Perturbation}_k + (1-\beta)b_k$. The only difference lies in the form of their respective perturbation terms. \textbf{Step 3: Compare relative bounds of the perturbation terms.} The equivalence hinges on whether these different perturbation terms satisfy the same relative error property with respect to their own system's state. For system $\{c_k\}$, the perturbation term is $\beta e_{k-1}$. Using the bound from \eqref{eq:error_bounds}: \begin{equation*} |\text{Perturbation}_c| = |\beta e_{k-1}| = \beta|e_{k-1}| \le \beta q |c_{k-1}|. \end{equation*} For system $\{a'_k\}$, the effective perturbation term is $\beta(1-\beta)d_{k-1}$. Using the bound from \eqref{eq:error_bounds} and the scaling relationship $a_{k-1} = a'_{k-1}/(1-\beta)$: \begin{equation*} |\text{Perturbation}_a| = |\beta(1-\beta)d_{k-1}| = \beta(1-\beta)|d_{k-1}| \le \beta(1-\beta)q|a_{k-1}| = \beta(1-\beta)q\frac{|a'_{k-1}|}{1-\beta} = \beta q |a'_{k-1}|. \end{equation*} \textbf{Conclusion of Proof.} Both systems, $\{c_k\}$ and the scaled $\{a'_k\}$, adhere to the same mathematical dynamics. Their evolution is governed by an identical recurrence structure, and their respective perturbation terms are bounded by the exact same relative factor $\beta q$ with respect to their own previous state. Therefore, from an analytical standpoint, the two systems are indistinguishable. Any conclusion regarding the long-term behavior (e.g., convergence, stability) of $\{c_k\}$ under its perturbation model will apply directly to $\{a'_k\}$ (and thus proportionally to $\{a_k\}$) under its own perturbation model.
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (Equivalence of Perturbed Dynamical Systems)
nodes.statement_short: Rescale a_k by (1-beta) and compare recurrences: both perturbations are bounded by beta q times the own state.

nodes.statement: With Lemma \ref{lemma:dynamical_equivalence} established, we can now apply this general result to our specific case of Quantized Adam. The weighted-sum moment $\mb_t$ from our analysis corresponds to the abstract sequence $\{a_k\}$, while the standard weighted-average moment $\tilde{\mb}_t$ corresponds to $\{c_k\}$. The gradient term $\gb_t$ corresponds to $\{b_k\}$, and the relative quantization errors in both schemes are modeled by the perturbations $\{d_k\}$ and $\{e_k\}$ with the bound factor $q$. Lemma \ref{lemma:dynamical_equivalence} thus formally proves that analyzing the quantization of our weighted-sum moment $\mb_t$ is analytically equivalent to analyzing the quantization of the standard weighted-average moment $\tilde{\mb}_t$. This rigorously justifies our proof strategy and ensures that our theoretical findings are directly relevant to practical implementations of Quantized Adam. A parallel argument holds for the second moments $\vb_t$ and $\tilde{\vb}_t$ with decay factor $\beta_2$.

nodes.statement:
The proof consists of two parts. 	extbf{Part 1: Bounding $v_{t,i}$} The update rule for the second moment estimate is $v_{t, i} =  eta_2 (v_{t-1, i} + 	heta_{t-1,i}) + (
abla_i f_t(\wb_{t-1}) + \delta_{t,i})^2$. The quantization noise is assumed to be a relative error, bounded by $|	heta_{t-1,i}| \le q_V|v_{t-1,i}|$. This implies that $(1-q_V)v_{t-1,i} \le v_{t-1,i} + 	heta_{t-1,i} \le (1+q_V)v_{t-1,i}$. Applying this to the update rule, we can establish the lower bound by recursively unrolling the inequality:  egin{align} v_{t, i} &\geq eta_2(1-q_V) v_{t-1, i} + (
abla_i f_t(\wb_{t-1}) + \delta_{t,i})^2 
onumber\ &\geq eta_2(1-q_V) \left[  eta_2(1-q_V)v_{t-2,i} + (
abla_i f_{t-1}(\wb_{t-2}) + \delta_{t-1,i})^2 ight] + (
abla_i f_t(\wb_{t-1}) + \delta_{t,i})^2 
onumber\ &= \dots 
onumber\ &=\sum_{k=0}^t eta_2^{t-k}(1-q_V)^{t-k}(
abla_i f_k(\wb_{k-1}) + \delta_{k,i})^2 \end{align} Similarly, we can establish the upper bound:  egin{align} v_{t, i} &\le eta_2(1+q_V) v_{t-1, i} + (
abla_i f_t(\wb_{t-1}) + \delta_{t,i})^2 
onumber\ &=\sum_{k=0}^t eta_2^{t-k}(1+q_V)^{t-k}(
abla_i f_k(\wb_{k-1}) + \delta_{k,i})^2 \end{align} This completes the proof of the first statement in the lemma. 	extbf{Part 2: Bounding the difference of the inverse square roots} Let $v'_{t,i}$ be the idealized second moment estimate, updated without the quantization noise $	heta$. Its explicit form is:  egin{align} v'_{t,i} = \sum_{k=0}^t eta_2^{t-k}(
abla_i f_k(\wb_{k-1}) + \delta_{k,i})^2 \end{align} From Part 1, we know that $v_{t,i}$ is in the interval $[LB_{t,i}, UB_{t,i}]$, where $LB_{t,i}$ and $UB_{t,i}$ are the bounds established. Now, we compare $v'_{t,i}$ with these bounds. Since $0 <  eta_2 < 1$ and we assume $0 < q_V < 1$, we have $ eta_2(1-q_V) <  eta_2 <  eta_2(1+q_V)$. This implies a term-by-term inequality, leading to:  egin{align} LB_{t,i} < v'_{t,i} < UB_{t,i} \end{align} Consider the function $f(y) = 1/\sqrt{\epsilon+y}$ for $y \ge 0$. This function is monotonically decreasing and convex. The value $v_{t,i}$ lies in the interval $[LB_{t,i}, UB_{t,i}]$, and $v'_{t,i}$ is a point within this interval. The maximum absolute difference $|f(v_{t,i}) - f(v'_{t,i})|$ must occur when $v_{t,i}$ is at one of the endpoints of the interval. Therefore, we can bound the difference as:  egin{align} \left| rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t,i}}}- rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}}ight| &\le \max\left\{ \left| rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}} -  rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}}ight|, \left| rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+UB_{t,i}}} -  rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}}ight| ight\} \end{align} Since $LB_{t,i} < v'_{t,i} < UB_{t,i}$ and the function is decreasing, we have $1/\sqrt{\epsilon+UB_{t,i}} < 1/\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}} < 1/\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}$. We can therefore remove the absolute value signs:  egin{align} \left| rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t,i}}}- rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}}ight| &\le \max\left\{  rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}} -  rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}},  rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}} -  rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+UB_{t,i}}} ight\} \end{align} This completes the proof of the second statement.
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (value range of v_{t,i})
nodes.statement_short: Unroll the second-moment recursion with relative errors for both bounds, then use monotonicity of 1/sqrt(eps+y).

nodes.statement: Given two discrete-time systems defined for \( t \ge 1 \): \begin{itemize} \item System A: \( a_{t}=k(a_{t-1}+c_{t-1})+d_{t} \) \item System B: \( b_{t}=kb_{t-1}+d_{t} \) \end{itemize} where the perturbation term \( c_t \) is bounded by \( |c_{t}|\le q|a_{t}| \) for all \( t \), and the constants \( k, q \) satisfy \( 0<k<1 \) and \( q<k \). Under zero initial conditions, where \( a_0 = b_0 = 0 \), the absolute error between the states of the two systems is bounded by: \begin{align} |a_{t}-b_{t}|\le\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}\left[(k(1+q))^{t-j}-k^{t-j}\right]|d_{j}| \end{align}
nodes.name: Bound on Discrete Error
assumptions: the perturbation term \( c_t \) is bounded by \( |c_{t}|\le q|a_{t}| \) for all \( t \)
the constants \( k, q \) satisfy \( 0<k<1 \) and \( q<k \)
Under zero initial conditions, where \( a_0 = b_0 = 0 \)
nodes.statement_short: Error between a relatively perturbed linear recursion and the unperturbed one is a weighted sum of inputs.
nodes.label: app:lemma:discrete_error_bound

nodes.statement: First, define the error as \( e_t = a_t - b_t \). Subtracting the two system equations yields the error recurrence relation: \begin{align} e_{t} = ke_{t-1} + kc_{t-1} \end{align} The explicit solution to this recurrence is \( e_{t} = k^{t}e_{0} + \sum_{j=0}^{t-1}k^{t-j}c_{j} \). Under the zero initial condition \( a_0 = b_0 = 0 \), this simplifies to: \begin{align} e_{t} = \sum_{j=0}^{t-1}k^{t-j}c_{j} \end{align} Taking the absolute value and applying the given condition \( |c_j| \le q|a_j| \), we have: \begin{align} |e_{t}| \le \sum_{j=0}^{t-1}k^{t-j}|c_{j}| \le q\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}k^{t-j}|a_{j}| \end{align} Since \( a_0=0 \), the sum starts from \( j=1 \). The state \( |a_j| \) can be bounded from its own recurrence \( |a_{t}| \le k(1+q)|a_{t-1}| + |d_t| \), which for \( a_0=0 \) unrolls to: \begin{align} |a_{j}|\le\sum_{i=1}^{j}(k(1+q))^{j-i}|d_{i}| \end{align} Substituting the bound for \( |a_j| \) into the inequality for \( |e_t| \) gives a double summation: \begin{align} |e_{t}|\le q\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}k^{t-j}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{j}(k(1+q))^{j-i}|d_{i}|\right) \end{align} By swapping the order of summation and evaluating the inner geometric series, we obtain the final result: \begin{align} |a_{t}-b_{t}| \le \sum_{j=1}^{t-1}\left[(k(1+q))^{t-j}-k^{t-j}\right]|d_{j}| \end{align}
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (Bound on Discrete Error)
nodes.statement_short: Solve the error recurrence explicitly, bound states by their own unrolled recursion, swap summation order.

nodes.statement: |e_{t}|\le q\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}k^{t-j}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{j}(k(1+q))^{j-i}|d_{i}|\right)

nodes.statement: Let \((g_k)_{k=0}^t\) be a sequence of scalars for any finite \(t \in \mathbb{N}\). Let the weights be terms of two geometric series, \(A_k = a^k\) and \(B_k = b^k\), where \(a, b \in (0, 1)\) are the base ratios. If the condition \(a^2 < b\) holds, then the ratio of the weighted sum is bounded by a constant derived from the corresponding infinite series: \begin{align} \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{t} a^k |g_k|}{\sqrt{\sum_{k=0}^{t} b^k g_k^2}} \le \sqrt{\frac{1}{1 - a^2/b}} \end{align}
nodes.name: Finite Geometric Series Ratio Bounded by Infinite Sum
assumptions: Let \((g_k)_{k=0}^t\) be a sequence of scalars for any finite \(t \in \mathbb{N}\)
the condition \(a^2 < b\) holds
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz bound: a^k-weighted l1 sum over sqrt of b^k-weighted l2 sum is at most 1/sqrt(1-a^2/b).
nodes.label: app:lemma:cauchy

nodes.statement: \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{t} a^k |g_k|}{\sqrt{\sum_{k=0}^{t} b^k g_k^2}} \le \sqrt{\frac{1}{1 - a^2/b}}
nodes.name: Equation (61)

nodes.statement: Let the numerator be \(N_t = \sum_{k=0}^{t} a^k |g_k|\) and the denominator be \(D_t = \sqrt{\sum_{k=0}^{t} b^k g_k^2}\). We rewrite the numerator as: \begin{align} N_t = \sum_{k=0}^{t} \left( \frac{a^k}{\sqrt{b^k}} \right) \cdot \left( \sqrt{b^k} |g_k| \right) \end{align} Applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to these finite sums, we get: \begin{align} N_t^2 &\le \left( \sum_{k=0}^{t} \left( \frac{a^k}{\sqrt{b^k}} \right)^2 \right) \cdot \left( \sum_{k=0}^{t} \left( \sqrt{b^k} |g_k| \right)^2 \right) \nonumber\\ &= \left( \sum_{k=0}^{t} \frac{a^{2k}}{b^k} \right) \cdot \left( \sum_{k=0}^{t} b^k g_k^2 \right) \nonumber\\ &= \left( \sum_{k=0}^{t} \left(\frac{a^2}{b}\right)^k \right) \cdot D_t^2 \end{align} The first term is a finite geometric series. Since the condition \(a^2 < b\) implies that the ratio \(r = a^2/b\) is positive and less than 1, all terms in the series are positive. Therefore, the finite sum is always less than or equal to the sum of the infinite series: \begin{align} \sum_{k=0}^{t} \left(\frac{a^2}{b}\right)^k \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{a^2}{b}\right)^k = \frac{1}{1 - a^2/b} \end{align} Substituting this upper bound back into the inequality for \(N_t^2\), we have: \begin{align} N_t^2 \le \left( \frac{1}{1 - a^2/b} \right) \cdot D_t^2 \end{align} Taking the square root of both sides gives: \begin{align} N_t \le \sqrt{\frac{1}{1 - a^2/b}} \cdot D_t \end{align} Finally, dividing by \(D_t\) yields the desired result for any finite \(t\): \begin{align} \frac{N_t}{D_t} = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{t} a^k |g_k|}{\sqrt{\sum_{k=0}^{t} b^k g_k^2}} \le \sqrt{\frac{1}{1 - a^2/b}} \end{align}
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (Finite Geometric Series Ratio)
nodes.statement_short: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the numerator split as (a^k/sqrt(b^k))(sqrt(b^k)|g_k|) and bound the geometric series.

nodes.statement: Let \((g_k)_{k=0}^t\) be a sequence of scalars. Let the weights be $A_k = \beta_1^k((1+q_M)^k - 1)$ and $B_k = (\beta_2(1-q_V))^k$. If the condition $\beta_1^2(1+q_M)^2 < \beta_2(1-q_V)$ holds, then the ratio of the weighted sum is bounded by: $$ \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{t} A_k |g_k|}{\sqrt{\sum_{k=0}^{t} B_k g_k^2}} \le q_M \cdot \frac{\sqrt{r'(1+r')}}{(1+q_M)(1-r')^{3/2}} $$ where $r' = \frac{\beta_1^2(1+q_M)^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}$.

nodes.statement:
Let the stochastic gradient be bounded in infinity norm almost surely by $
orm{
abla f_t(\wb; \gamma)}_\infty \le R - \sqrt{\epsilon}$ for any parameters $\wb$. Let the gradient quantization operator satisfy the relative error model $|Q(z) - z| \le q_G|z|$ for any scalar $z$. The quantized gradient estimator $\hat{\gb_t}$ is defined component-wise for $i \in [d]$ as:  egin{align} \hat{g}_{t,i} =  rac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^{B} [
abla^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j})]_i, \end{align} where we use $
abla^Q f(\cdot)$ as shorthand for $Q(
abla f(\cdot))$ and $[\cdot]_i$ to denote the i-th component. Then, the infinity norm of the estimator is bounded almost surely:  egin{align} 
orm{\hat{\gb_t}}_\infty \le (1+q_G)(R - \sqrt{\epsilon}). \end{align} For notational simplicity in subsequent proofs, we will use the slightly looser bound $
orm{\hat{\gb_t}}_\infty \le (1+q_G)R$.
nodes.name: Bound on the Quantized Gradient Estimator
assumptions: Let the stochastic gradient be bounded in infinity norm almost surely by $\norm{\nabla f_t(\wb; \gamma)}_\infty \le R - \sqrt{\epsilon}$ for any parameters $\wb$
Let the gradient quantization operator satisfy the relative error model $|Q(z) - z| \le q_G|z|$ for any scalar $z$
nodes.statement_short: The averaged quantized stochastic gradient has l_inf norm at most (1+q_G)(R - sqrt(eps)).
nodes.label: lemma:grad_bound

nodes.statement:
We first bound the infinity norm of a single quantized gradient vector $
abla^Q f(\cdot)$. For any component $i \in [d]$, we have:  egin{align} \left| 
abla_i^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) ight| &= \left| 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) + \left(
abla_i^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) - 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j})ight) ight| 
onumber \ &\le \left| 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) ight| + \left| 
abla_i^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) - 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) ight| 
onumber \ &\le \left| 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) ight| + q_G \left| 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) ight| 
onumber \ &= (1+q_G) \left| 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) ight|. \end{align} Since this holds for any component, it also holds for the component with the maximum absolute value. Therefore, by taking the maximum over $i \in [d]$, we can bound the infinity norm:  egin{align} 
orm{
abla^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j})}_\infty &\le (1+q_G) 
orm{
abla f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j})}_\infty 
onumber \ &\le (1+q_G) (R - \sqrt{\epsilon}). \end{align} Finally, we apply the triangle inequality to the full estimator $\hat{\gb_t}$, which is the average over $B$ such vectors:  egin{align} 
orm{\hat{\gb_t}}_\infty &= 
orm{ rac{1}{B} \sum_{j=1}^{B} 
abla^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j})}_\infty 
onumber \ &\le  rac{1}{B} \sum_{j=1}^{B} 
orm{
abla^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j})}_\infty 
onumber \ &\le  rac{1}{B} \sum_{j=1}^{B} (1+q_G) (R - \sqrt{\epsilon}) 
onumber \ &= (1+q_G) (R - \sqrt{\epsilon}). \end{align} This concludes the proof.
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (Bound on the Quantized Gradient Estimator)
nodes.statement_short: Relative error gives (1+q_G) times each component, then triangle inequality over the batch average.

nodes.statement: Assume we have $0 < \beta_1 < \beta_2 \leq 1$ and a sequence of real numbers $(a_n)_{n\in \NN^*}$. We define for all $n \in \NN^*$: $$b_n = \sum_{j=1}^n \beta_2^{n - j} a_j^2 \quad \text{and} \quad c_n = \sum_{j=1}^n \beta_1^{n-j} a_j.$$ Then for any $\epsilon > 0$, we have the following inequality: \begin{equation} \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{c_j^2}{\epsilon + b_j} \leq \frac{1}{(1 - \beta_1)(1 - \beta_1 / \beta_2)} \left(\ln\left(1 + \frac{b_n}{\epsilon}\right) - n\ln(\beta_2)\right). \end{equation}
nodes.name: Lemma A.2 of Defossez et al. (sum of ratios)
assumptions: Assume we have $0 < \beta_1 < \beta_2 \leq 1$ and a sequence of real numbers $(a_n)_{n\in \NN^*}$
for any $\epsilon > 0$
nodes.statement_short: Sum of c_j^2/(eps+b_j) for momentum c and EMA b is bounded by log(1+b_n/eps) - n log beta2 over (1-beta1)(1-beta1/beta2).

nodes.statement: \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{c_j^2}{\epsilon + b_j} \leq \frac{1}{(1 - \beta_1)(1 - \beta_1 / \beta_2)} \left(\ln\left(1 + \frac{b_n}{\epsilon}\right) - n\ln(\beta_2)\right).
nodes.name: Equation (108)
nodes.label: eq:sum_ratio_combined_lemma7

nodes.statement: First, we use Jensen's inequality on $c_j^2$, noting that $\sum_{l=1}^j \beta_1^{j-l} = \frac{1-\beta_1^j}{1-\beta_1} \leq \frac{1}{1-\beta_1}$, to get: \begin{align*} c_{j}^2 = \left(\sum_{l=1}^j \beta_1^{j - l}a_l\right)^2 \leq \left(\sum_{l=1}^j \beta_1^{j-l}\right) \left(\sum_{l=1}^j \beta_1^{j - l}a_l^2\right) \leq \frac{1}{1 - \beta_1}\sum_{l=1}^j \beta_1^{j - l}a_l^2. \end{align*} Dividing by $\epsilon + b_j$ and using the fact that for $l \leq j$, $b_j \geq \beta_2^{j-l}b_l$, which implies $\epsilon + b_j \geq \beta_2^{j-l}(\epsilon + b_l)$, we obtain: \begin{align} \frac{c_{j}^2}{\epsilon + b_{j}} \leq \frac{1}{1 - \beta_1}\sum_{l=1}^j \beta_1^{j - l} \frac{a_l^2}{\epsilon + b_j} \leq \frac{1}{1 - \beta_1}\sum_{l=1}^j \left(\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_2}\right)^{j-l}\frac{a_l^2}{\epsilon + b_l}. \end{align} Now, we sum over $j \in [n]$ and swap the order of summation: \begin{align} \nonumber \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{c_{j}^2}{\epsilon + b_{j}} &\leq \frac{1}{1 - \beta_1}\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{l=1}^{j}\left(\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_2}\right)^{j -l} \frac{a_{l}^2}{\epsilon + b_{l}} = \frac{1}{1 - \beta_1}\sum_{l=1}^n\frac{a_l^2}{\epsilon + b_l}\sum_{j=l}^{n}\left(\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_2}\right)^{j -l} \\ &\leq \frac{1}{(1 - \beta_1)(1 - \beta_1 /\beta_2)}\sum_{l=1}^n\frac{a_l^2}{\epsilon + b_l}, \end{align} where the last step uses the sum of a geometric series, since $\beta_1/\beta_2 < 1$. The next step is to bound the final sum. Let's denote $x_l = a_l^2$. The sum is $\sum_{l=1}^n \frac{x_l}{\epsilon + b_l}$, where $b_l = \sum_{k=1}^l \beta_2^{l-k}x_k$. Note that $b_l - x_l = \beta_2 b_{l-1}$ (with $b_0=0$). Using the inequality $\frac{x}{y} \leq \ln(y) - \ln(y-x)$ for $0 < x < y$, we have: \begin{align*} \frac{x_l}{\epsilon + b_l} &\leq \ln(\epsilon + b_l) - \ln(\epsilon + b_l - x_l) \\ &= \ln(\epsilon + b_l) - \ln(\epsilon + \beta_2 b_{l-1}) \\ &= \ln\left(\frac{\epsilon + b_l}{\epsilon + b_{l-1}}\right) + \ln\left(\frac{\epsilon + b_{l-1}}{\epsilon + \beta_2 b_{l-1}}\right). \end{align*} Summing from $l=1$ to $n$, the first term forms a telescoping series equal to $\ln(\epsilon + b_n) - \ln(\epsilon) = \ln(1 + b_n/\epsilon)$. For the second term, since $\beta_2 \leq 1$ and $b_{l-1} \geq 0$, we have $\frac{\epsilon + \beta_2 b_{l-1}}{\epsilon + b_{l-1}} \geq \beta_2$, which implies $\ln\left(\frac{\epsilon + b_{l-1}}{\epsilon + \beta_2 b_{l-1}}\right) \leq -\ln(\beta_2)$. Thus, summing over $l$ gives: \begin{equation} \sum_{l=1}^n\frac{a_l^2}{\epsilon + b_l} \leq \ln\left(1 + \frac{b_n}{\epsilon}\right) - n\ln(\beta_2). \end{equation} This inequality is a useful result in itself, corresponding to the special case where $c_j^2$ is replaced by $a_j^2$ (or equivalently $\beta_1 \to 0$ and $a_j$ is replaced by $a_j^2$). Finally, substituting the bound from \eqref{eq:special_case_bound_lemma7} into \eqref{eq:intermediate_bound_lemma7} yields the desired result.

nodes.statement: For any scalar $\rho \in (0, 1)$ and any integer $K \in \NN$, the following bound holds for the finite geometric sum: \begin{equation} \sum_{k = 0}^{K - 1} \rho^k \sqrt{k + 1} \leq \frac{2}{(1 - \rho)^{3/2}}. \end{equation}
nodes.name: Lemma A.3 of Defossez et al. (geometric sum with sqrt)
assumptions: For any scalar $\rho \in (0, 1)$ and any integer $K \in \NN$
nodes.label: app:lemma:sum_geom_sqrt

nodes.statement: Let the sum be denoted by $S_K = \sum_{k = 0}^{K - 1} \rho^k \sqrt{k + 1}$. We analyze the term $(1-\rho)S_K$: \begin{align*} (1 - \rho) S_K &= \sum_{k = 0}^{K - 1} \rho^k \sqrt{k+1} - \sum_{j = 1}^K \rho^{j} \sqrt{j} \\ &= 1 + \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \rho^k(\sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt{k}) - \rho^K\sqrt{K}. \end{align*} By the concavity of the square root function, $\sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt{k} \leq \frac{1}{2\sqrt{k}}$. This implies: \begin{align*} (1 - \rho) S_K &\leq 1 + \sum_{k = 1}^{K- 1} \frac{\rho^{k}}{2 \sqrt{k}} \leq 1 + \int_0^{\infty} \frac{\rho^{t}}{2 \sqrt{t}}\mathrm{d}t. \end{align*} The integral is a standard Gaussian integral form which evaluates to $\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2 \sqrt{-\ln(\rho)}}$. Using the inequality $-\ln(\rho) \geq 1 - \rho$, we have: \begin{align*} (1 - \rho) S_K \leq 1 + \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2 \sqrt{1-\rho}} \leq \frac{2}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}. \end{align*} Dividing by $(1-\rho)$ yields the desired result.

nodes.statement_short: Bound (1-rho)S_K by concavity of sqrt and a Gaussian-type integral.

nodes.statement: Let the sum be denoted by $S_K = \sum_{k = 0}^{K - 1} \rho^k \sqrt{k} (k + 1)$. We proceed by analyzing $(1-\rho)S_K$: \begin{align*} (1-\rho)S_K &= \sum_{k = 1}^{K - 1} \rho^k \left[ \sqrt{k} (k + 1) - k\sqrt{k - 1}\right] - \rho^K k \sqrt{K-1} \\ &\leq \sum_{k = 1}^{K - 1} \rho^k (2\sqrt{k}), \end{align*} where the inequality holds because $\sqrt{k} (k + 1) - k\sqrt{k - 1} \le 2\sqrt{k}$. Re-indexing the sum gives: \begin{align*} (1 - \rho) S_K &\leq 2 \rho \sum_{k = 1}^{K - 1} \rho^{k-1} \sqrt{k} = 2 \rho \sum_{j = 0}^{K - 2} \rho^j \sqrt{j + 1}. \end{align*} Applying the result from Lemma~\ref{app:lemma:sum_geom_sqrt} to the final sum, we get: \begin{align*} (1 - \rho) S_K \leq 2 \rho \left( \frac{2}{(1 - \rho)^{3/2}} \right) = \frac{4 \rho}{(1 - \rho)^{3/2}}. \end{align*} Dividing both sides by $(1-\rho)$ completes the proof.

abla F(\Wb_t)\|_* - 2\eta\sqrt{r}\|

nodes.statement: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assump:smooth} and \ref{assump:bound_init} hold. The iterates of Muon satisfy that for any $t\ge 0$, \begin{align*} \|\Wb_t\|_F \le D+t\eta\sqrt{r},\quad \|\nabla F(\Wb_t)\|_F \le G + t\eta\sqrt{r}L. \end{align*}
nodes.name: Bound of ||W||_F and ||grad F(W)||_F for Muon
assumptions: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assump:smooth} and \ref{assump:bound_init} hold
nodes.label: lemma:muon_bounded_w_grad

nodes.statement:
According to the update of Muon, we have  egin{align*} & \|\Wb_t\|_F \ =& \|\Wb_{t-1} - \eta\Ub_t\Vb_t^{	op}\|_F \ \le& \|\Wb_{t-1}\|_F + \eta \|\Ub_t\Vb_t^{	op}\|_F \ =& \|\Wb_{t-1}\|_F + \eta\sqrt{	r(\Vb_t\Ub_t^{	op}\Ub_t\Vb_t^{	op})} \ \le& \|\Wb_{t-1}\|_F + \eta\sqrt{r} \ \le& \|\Wb_0\|_F + t\eta\sqrt{r} \ \le& D + t\eta\sqrt{r}. \end{align*} The third inequality is because $\Ub_t$ and $\Vb_t$ are orthogonal matrices, and the last inequality is due to Assumption~ef{assump:bound_init}.  egin{align*} & \|
abla F(\Wb_t)\|_F \ \le& \|
abla F(\Wb_0)\|_F + \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \|
abla F(\Wb_{k+1}) - 
abla F(\Wb_k)\|_F \ \le& G + \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} L\|\Wb_{k+1} - \Wb_k\|_F \ \le& G + \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} L\eta\sqrt{r} \ =& G + t\eta\sqrt{r}L. \end{align*} The first inequality is due to the triangle inequality, the second inequality is due to Assumption~ef{assump:smooth}, and the last inequality is due to the update of Muon.
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (Muon weight and gradient bounds)
nodes.statement_short: Each Muon step moves W by at most eta sqrt(r) in Frobenius norm; smoothness transfers this to the gradient.

nodes.statement: Suppose Assumption~\ref{assump:qe} holds. For any matrix $\Xb\in\RR^{m\times n}$ and its quantized version $\Xb^Q$, we have \begin{align*} \|\Xb^{Q} - \Xb\|_F \le q\|\Xb\|_F. \end{align*}
nodes.name: Matrix relative quantization error
assumptions: Suppose Assumption~\ref{assump:qe} holds
nodes.label: lemma:muon_mat_qe

nodes.statement: According to Assumption~\ref{assump:qe}, we have \begin{align*} \|\Xb^Q - \Xb\|_F^2 =& \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n |X_{ij}^Q - X_{ij}|^2 \\ \le& \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n q^2|X_{ij}|^2 \\ =& q^2\|\Xb\|_F^2. \end{align*} Taking the square root on both sides, we complete the proof.
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (matrix relative quantization error)
nodes.statement_short: Sum the elementwise relative error bound over entries.

nodes.statement: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assump:smooth} and \ref{assump:bound_init} hold. For any $t\ge 0$, we have \begin{align*} \EE[\|\nabla F(\Wb_t)-\Cb_t\|_F] \le \frac{\beta L \eta \sqrt{r}}{1-\beta}. \end{align*}
nodes.name: Momentum bias bound for Muon
assumptions: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assump:smooth} and \ref{assump:bound_init} hold
nodes.label: lemma:muon_GC

nodes.statement:
This proof is a standard technique for bounding the bias term of momentum. We have  egin{align*} &\EE[\|
abla F(\Wb_t)-\Cb_t\|_F]
otag\ =&\EE[\|
abla F(\Wb_t)-( eta \Cb_{t-1}+(1- eta)
abla F(\Wb_t))\|_F]
otag\ =&\EE[ eta\|
abla F(\Wb_t)-\Cb_{t-1}\|_F]
otag\ \le&\EE[ eta\|
abla F(\Wb_{t-1})-\Cb_{t-1}\|_F+ eta\|
abla F(\Wb_{t-1})-
abla F(\Wb_t)\|_F]
otag\ \le&\EE[ eta\|
abla F(\Wb_{t-1})-\Cb_{t-1}\|_F + eta L\|\Wb_{t-1}-\Wb_t\|_F]
otag\ =&\EE[ eta\|
abla F(\Wb_{t-1})-\Cb_{t-1}\|_F+ eta L \eta\|\Ub_{t-1}\Vb_{t-1}^	op\|_F]
otag\ \le&\EE[ eta\|
abla F(\Wb_{t-1})-\Cb_{t-1}\|_F+ eta L \eta \sqrt{r}]
otag\ \le& eta^t\|
abla F(\Wb_0)-\Cb_0\|_F+\sum_{i=1}^t  eta^i L \eta \sqrt{r} 
otag\ \le&  rac{ eta L \eta \sqrt{r}}{1- eta}. \end{align*}
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (momentum bias)
nodes.statement_short: Standard momentum bias recursion using L-smoothness and the bounded Muon step.

nodes.statement: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assump:grad_unbiased} and~\ref{assump:grad_bounds} hold. For any $t\ge 0$, we have \begin{align*} \EE[\|\Cb_t - \Xb_t\|_F] \le \beta^t\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{B}} + \sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{B}}. \end{align*}
nodes.name: Stochastic variance of momentum for Muon
assumptions: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assump:grad_unbiased} and~\ref{assump:grad_bounds} hold
nodes.label: lemma:muon_CX

nodes.statement:
Expanding $\Cb_t$ and $\Xb_t$ by their definitions in \eqref{eq:muon_C} and \eqref{eq:muon_X}, we have  egin{align*} \Cb_t =&  eta^t\Cb_0 + (1- eta)\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}
abla F(\Wb_k) , \ \Xb_t =&  eta^t\Xb_0 + (1- eta)\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k} rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla f(\Wb_k; xi_{k,i}). \end{align*} Thus, we have  egin{align*} &\EE[\|\Cb_t - \Xb_t\|_F] \ \le& \EE[\| eta^t(\Cb_0 - \Xb_0)\|_F] + \EE[(1- eta)\|\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}(
abla F(\Wb_k)- rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla f(\Wb_k; xi_{k,i}))\|_F] \ \le&  eta^t\EE[\|\Cb_0 - \Xb_0\|_F] + \sqrt{\EE[(1- eta)^2\|\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}(
abla F(\Wb_k)- rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla f(\Wb_k; xi_{k,i}))\|_F^2]} \ =&  eta^t\EE[\|\Cb_0 - \Xb_0\|_F] + \sqrt{\EE[(1- eta)^2\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{2(t-k)} rac{1}{B^2}\sum_{i=1}^B\|
abla F(\Wb_k; xi_{k,i})-
abla F(\Wb_k)\|_F^2]} \ \le&  eta^t\EE[\|\Cb_0 - \Xb_0\|_F] + \sqrt{(1- eta)^2\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{2(t-k)} rac{\sigma^2}{B}} \ \le&  eta^t rac{\sigma}{\sqrt{B}} + \sqrt{ rac{1- eta}{1+ eta}} rac{\sigma}{\sqrt{B}}. \end{align*} The second inequality is due to Jensen's inequality, the first equality is due to the independence of $ xi_{k,i}$ for different $k$ or $i$, and the third inequality is due to Assumptions~ef{assump:grad_unbiased} and~ef{assump:grad_bounds}.
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (stochastic variance)
nodes.statement_short: Unroll both momenta, apply Jensen and independence of the samples to bound the variance.

nodes.statement: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assump:grad_unbiased},~\ref{assump:grad_bounds} and \ref{assump:qe} hold. For any $t\ge 0$, we have \begin{align*} \EE[\|\Xb_t - \Yb_t\|_F] \le q_G(\sigma + G + t\eta\sqrt{r}L). \end{align*}
nodes.name: Gradient quantization error of momentum for Muon
assumptions: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assump:grad_unbiased},~\ref{assump:grad_bounds} and \ref{assump:qe} hold
nodes.label: lemma:muon_XY

nodes.statement:
By the definition of $\Xb_t$ and $\Yb_t$ in \eqref{eq:muon_X} and \eqref{eq:muon_Y}, we have  egin{align*} &\EE[\| \Xb_t - \Yb_t \|_F]
otag\ \le& \EE[ eta \| \Xb_{t-1} - \Yb_{t-1} \|_F] + (1- eta) rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B\EE[\| 
abla f(\Wb_t; xi_{t,i}) - 
abla^Q f(\Wb_t; xi_{t,i}) \|_F] 
otag \ \le& \EE[ eta \| \Xb_{t-1} - \Yb_{t-1} \|_F] + (1- eta) rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B\EE[ q_G\| 
abla f(\Wb_t; xi_{t,i}) \|_F] 
otag \ \le& \EE[ eta \| \Xb_{t-1} - \Yb_{t-1} \|_F] + (1- eta)\EE[ q_G(\sigma + \| 
abla F(\Wb_t) \|_F )] 
otag \ \le& \EE[ eta \| \Xb_{t-1} - \Yb_{t-1} \|_F] + (1- eta) q_G(\sigma + G + t\eta\sqrt{r}L ) 
otag \ \le&  eta^t\|\Xb_0 - \Yb_0\|_F + (1- eta) q_G(\sigma + G + t\eta\sqrt{r}L )\sum_{k=0}^{t-1} eta^k 
otag \ \le&  eta^t q_G(\sigma + G) + (1- eta^t) q_G(\sigma + G + t\eta\sqrt{r}L ) 
otag \ \le& q_G(\sigma + G) + (1- eta^t)q_G t\eta\sqrt{r}L 
otag \ \le& q_G(\sigma + G + t\eta\sqrt{r}L ). \end{align*} The second inequality is due to Assumption~ef{assump:qe}, Lemma~ef{lemma:muon_mat_qe} and Definition~ef{eq:muon_var_qe}. The third inequality is due to Assumption~ef{assump:grad_bounds}. The fourth inequality is due to Lemma~ef{lemma:muon_bounded_w_grad}.
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (gradient quantization error)
nodes.statement_short: Recursive bound using the relative gradient error, the variance bound and the gradient growth lemma.

nodes.statement: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assump:grad_unbiased},~\ref{assump:grad_bounds},~\ref{assump:smooth} and \ref{assump:qe} hold. For any $t\ge 0$, we have \begin{align*} \EE[\|\Yb_t - \Zb_t\|_F] \le& \beta^t\cdot\frac{2\sigma}{\sqrt{B}} + \sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}}\cdot\frac{2\sigma}{\sqrt{B}} + 2q_G(\sigma + G) + 2q_G t\eta\sqrt{r}L + \\ & q_W(1+q_G)DL + q_W(1+q_G)t\eta\sqrt{r}L, \\ \EE[\|\Zb_t\|_F] \le& \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{B}} + \sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}}\cdot\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{B}} + G + q_G(\sigma + G) + q_W (1+q_G)DL + \\ & (1+q_W)(1+q_G)t\eta\sqrt{r}L. \end{align*}

assumptions: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assump:grad_unbiased},~\ref{assump:grad_bounds},~\ref{assump:smooth} and \ref{assump:qe} hold
conclusions: \EE[\|\Yb_t - \Zb_t\|_F] \le& \beta^t\cdot\frac{2\sigma}{\sqrt{B}} + \sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}}\cdot\frac{2\sigma}{\sqrt{B}} + 2q_G(\sigma + G) + 2q_G t\eta\sqrt{r}L + \\ & q_W(1+q_G)DL + q_W(1+q_G)t\eta\sqrt{r}L, \\ \EE[\|\Zb_t\|_F] \le& \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{B}} + \sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}}\cdot\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{B}} + G + q_G(\sigma + G) + q_W (1+q_G)DL + \\ & (1+q_W)(1+q_G)t\eta\sqrt{r}L.
nodes.label: lemma:muon_YZ

nodes.statement:
By the definition of $\Yb_t$ and $\Zb_t$ in \eqref{eq:muon_Y} and \eqref{eq:muon_Z}, we have  egin{align*} \Yb_t =&  eta^t\Yb_0 + (1- eta)\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k} rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla^Q f(\Wb_k; xi_{k,i}) , \ \Zb_t =&  eta^t\Zb_0 + (1- eta)\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k} rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla^Q f(\Wb_k^Q; xi_{k,i}) . \end{align*} Thus, by the triangle inequality, we have  egin{align} &\EE[\| \Yb_t - \Zb_t \|_F]
otag\ \le& \EE[ eta^t \| \Yb_{0} - \Zb_{0} \|_F] + (1- eta)\EE[\|\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}\cdot( rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B 
abla^Q f(\Wb_k; xi_{k,i}) - 
abla^Q f(\Wb_k^Q; xi_{k,i}) ) \|_F] 
otag \ \le& \EE[ eta^t \| \Yb_{0} - \Zb_{0} \|_F] + \underbrace{(1- eta)\EE[\|\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}\cdot( rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B 
abla^Q f(\Wb_k; xi_{k,i}) -
abla f(\Wb_k; xi_{k,i}) \|_F]}_{	ext{\large A}} + 
otag \ & \underbrace{(1- eta)\EE[\|\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}\cdot( rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla f(\Wb_k; xi_{k,i}) - 
abla F(\Wb_k))\|_F]}_{	ext{\large C}} + 
otag \ & \underbrace{(1- eta)\EE[\|\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}\cdot(
abla F(\Wb_k) - 
abla F(\Wb_k^Q))\|_F]}_{	ext{\large H}} + 
otag \ & \underbrace{(1- eta) \EE[\|\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}\cdot(
abla F(\Wb_k^Q) -  rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla f(\Wb_k^Q; xi_{k,i}) ) \|_F]}_{	ext{\large I}} + 
otag \ & \underbrace{(1- eta) \EE[\|\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}\cdot( rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla f(\Wb_k^Q; xi_{k,i}) - 
abla^Q f(\Wb_k^Q; xi_{k,i}) ) \|_F]}_{	ext{\large J}}. \end{align} Next, we bound each term in \eqref{eq:muon_YZ_decomp} one by one. \paragraph{Bound on $ eta^t \EE[\| \Yb_{0} - \Zb_{0} \|_F]$.} By the definitions of $\Yb_0$ and $\Zb_0$ in \eqref{eq:muon_Y} and \eqref{eq:muon_Z}, we have  egin{align*} \Yb_0 =&  rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla^Q f(\Wb_0; xi_{0,i}), \ \Zb_0 =&  rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla^Q f(\Wb_0^Q; xi_{0,i}). \end{align*} Thus, we have  egin{align} & eta^t \EE[\| \Yb_{0} - \Zb_{0} \|_F] 
otag \ =&  eta^t \EE[\| rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla^Q f(\Wb_0; xi_{0,i}) -  rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla^Q f(\Wb_0^Q; xi_{0,i})\|_F] 
otag \ \le&  eta^t  rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B \EE[\|
abla^Q f(\Wb_0; xi_{0,i}) - 
abla f(\Wb_0; xi_{0,i})\|_F] + 
otag \ &  eta^t \EE[\| rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla f(\Wb_0; xi_{0,i}) - 
abla F(\Wb_0)\|_F] + 
otag \ &  eta^t \EE[\|
abla F(\Wb_0) - 
abla F(\Wb_0^Q)\|_F] + 
otag \ &  eta^t \EE[\| rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla F(\Wb_0^Q) - 
abla f(\Wb_0^Q; xi_{0,i}) \|_F] + 
otag \ &  eta^t  rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B \EE[\|
abla f(\Wb_0^Q; xi_{0,i}) - 
abla^Q f(\Wb_0^Q; xi_{0,i}) \|_F] 
otag \ \le&  eta^t rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B q_G\EE[\|
abla f(\Wb_0; xi_{0,i})\|_F] +  eta^t rac{\sigma}{\sqrt{B}} +  eta^t L q_W\EE[\|\Wb_0\|_F] +  eta^t rac{\sigma}{\sqrt{B}} + 
otag \ &  eta^t rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B q_G\EE[\|

The second inequality we used Definition~ef{eq:muon_var_qe} for the first and last terms, Assumption~ef{assump:grad_unbiased},~ef{assump:grad_bounds} and Jensen's inequality for the second and fourth terms, and Assumption~ef{assump:smooth} and Definition~ef{eq:muon_var_qe} for the third term. The third inequality is due to Assumption~ef{assump:grad_bounds},~ef{assump:bound_init} and Definition~ef{eq:muon_var_qe}. \paragraph{Bound on 	ext{\large A}.}  egin{align} A =& (1- eta)\EE[\|\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}\cdot( rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B

otag \ \le& (1- eta)\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k} rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B q_G(\sigma + \EE[\|

otag \ \le& (1- eta)\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k} rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B q_G(\sigma + G + t\eta\sqrt{r}L) 
otag \ =& (1- eta^t)q_G(\sigma + G + t\eta\sqrt{r}L). \end{align} The first inequality is due to Definition~ef{eq:muon_var_qe} and the triangle inequality. otag \ \le& (1- eta)\sqrt{\EE[\|\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}\cdot( rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B 
abla f(\Wb_k; xi_{k,i}) -
abla F(\Wb_k) ) \|_F^2]} 
otag \ =& (1- eta)\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{2(t-k)} rac{1}{B^2}\sum_{i=1}^B\EE[\|

otag \ \le& (1- eta)\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}Lq_W\EE[\| \Wb_k \|_F]

otag \ \le& (1- eta^t)q_W L(D + t\eta\sqrt{r} ). \end{align} The first inequality is due to the triangle inequality. The second inequality is due to Assumption~ef{assump:smooth}. The third inequality is due to Definition~ef{eq:muon_var_qe}. The fourth inequality is due to Lemma~ef{lemma:muon_bounded_w_grad}. \paragraph{Bound on 	ext{\large I}.} Similar to Lemma~ef{lemma:muon_CX}, we have  egin{align} I =& (1- eta) \EE[\|\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}\cdot(
abla F(\Wb_k^Q) -  rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B
abla f(\Wb_k^Q; xi_{k,i}) ) \|_F] 
otag \ \le& (1- eta) \sqrt{ \EE[\|\sum_{k=1}^t eta^{t-k}\cdot(
