Plan: compare recurrences
nodes.statement: To prove the equivalence, we derive the recurrence relation for the scaled sequence $\{a'_k\}$ and compare its structure and error properties to that of $\{c_k\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Derive the scaled recurrence and compare with c_k.

nodes.name: Step 1: recurrence for a'_k
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 1: Derive the recurrence for $\{a'_k\}$.} Starting from the definition $a'_k = (1-\beta)a_k$ and substituting the dynamics from \eqref{eq:system_a}: \begin{align*} a'_k &= (1-\beta) \left[ \beta(a_{k-1} + d_{k-1}) + b_k \right] \\ &= \beta(1-\beta)a_{k-1} + \beta(1-\beta)d_{k-1} + (1-\beta)b_k. \end{align*} Now, we replace $a_{k-1}$ with $a'_{k-1}/(1-\beta)$: \begin{align*} a'_k &= \beta(1-\beta)\left(\frac{a'_{k-1}}{1-\beta}\right) + \beta(1-\beta)d_{k-1} + (1-\beta)b_k \\ &= \beta a'_{k-1} + \beta(1-\beta)d_{k-1} + (1-\beta)b_k. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the dynamics into a'_k = (1-beta)a_k.

nodes.name: Step 2: compare structures
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 2: Compare recurrence structures.} Let us place the recurrence relations for $\{c_k\}$ and $\{a'_k\}$ side-by-side: \begin{align*} c_k &= \beta c_{k-1} + \beta e_{k-1} + (1-\beta)b_k \\ a'_k &= \beta a'_{k-1} + \beta(1-\beta)d_{k-1} + (1-\beta)b_k. \end{align*} Both sequences share the identical structure: $X_k = \beta X_{k-1} + \text{Perturbation}_k + (1-\beta)b_k$. The only difference lies in the form of their respective perturbation terms.
nodes.statement_short: Both recurrences have the form X_k = beta X_{k-1} + perturbation + (1-beta)b_k.

nodes.name: Step 3: relative bounds of perturbations
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 3: Compare relative bounds of the perturbation terms.} The equivalence hinges on whether these different perturbation terms satisfy the same relative error property with respect to their own system's state. For system $\{c_k\}$, the perturbation term is $\beta e_{k-1}$. Using the bound from \eqref{eq:error_bounds}: \begin{equation*} |\text{Perturbation}_c| = |\beta e_{k-1}| = \beta|e_{k-1}| \le \beta q |c_{k-1}|. \end{equation*} For system $\{a'_k\}$, the effective perturbation term is $\beta(1-\beta)d_{k-1}$. Using the bound from \eqref{eq:error_bounds} and the scaling relationship $a_{k-1} = a'_{k-1}/(1-\beta)$: \begin{equation*} |\text{Perturbation}_a| = |\beta(1-\beta)d_{k-1}| = \beta(1-\beta)|d_{k-1}| \le \beta(1-\beta)q|a_{k-1}| = \beta(1-\beta)q\frac{|a'_{k-1}|}{1-\beta} = \beta q |a'_{k-1}|. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Both perturbations are bounded by beta q times the previous state.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: \textbf{Conclusion of Proof.} Both systems, $\{c_k\}$ and the scaled $\{a'_k\}$, adhere to the same mathematical dynamics. Their evolution is governed by an identical recurrence structure, and their respective perturbation terms are bounded by the exact same relative factor $\beta q$ with respect to their own previous state. Therefore, from an analytical standpoint, the two systems are indistinguishable. Any conclusion regarding the long-term behavior (e.g., convergence, stability) of $\{c_k\}$ under its perturbation model will apply directly to $\{a'_k\}$ (and thus proportionally to $\{a_k\}$) under its own perturbation model.
nodes.statement_short: The two systems are analytically indistinguishable.

nodes.name: Instantiate the lemma
nodes.statement: With Lemma \ref{lemma:dynamical_equivalence} established, we can now apply this general result to our specific case of Quantized Adam. The weighted-sum moment $\mb_t$ from our analysis corresponds to the abstract sequence $\{a_k\}$, while the standard weighted-average moment $\tilde{\mb}_t$ corresponds to $\{c_k\}$. The gradient term $\gb_t$ corresponds to $\{b_k\}$, and the relative quantization errors in both schemes are modeled by the perturbations $\{d_k\}$ and $\{e_k\}$ with the bound factor $q$.
nodes.statement_short: Map m_t to a_k, the weighted-average moment to c_k and gradients to b_k.

nodes.name: Conclude equivalence
nodes.statement: Lemma \ref{lemma:dynamical_equivalence} thus formally proves that analyzing the quantization of our weighted-sum moment $\mb_t$ is analytically equivalent to analyzing the quantization of the standard weighted-average moment $\tilde{\mb}_t$. This rigorously justifies our proof strategy and ensures that our theoretical findings are directly relevant to practical implementations of Quantized Adam. A parallel argument holds for the second moments $\vb_t$ and $\tilde{\vb}_t$ with decay factor $\beta_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Quantizing weighted-sum moments is equivalent; same for v_t.

nodes.name: Auxiliary moments and notation
nodes.statement:
To systematically analyze the effects of quantization, we begin by isolating the different sources of error. We introduce auxiliary moment estimates, $m'_{t,i}$ and $v'_{t,i}$, which are defined to incorporate the quantization error from the stochastic gradient, $\delta_{t,i}$, but are themselves assumed to be stored with perfect precision. Their dynamics are given by:  egin{equation}  egin{aligned} m'_{t, i} &= eta_1 m'_{t-1, i} + (
abla_i f_t(\wb_{t-1})+\delta_{t,i})\ v'_{t, i} &= eta_2 v'_{t-1, i} + (
abla_i f_t(\wb_{t-1})+\delta_{t,i})^2\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} Throughout the following proof we note $\espt{\cdot}$ the conditional expectation with respect to $f_1, \ldots, f_{t-1}$. In particular, $\wb_{t-1}$, $\vb_{t-1}$ is deterministic knowing $f_1, \ldots, f_{t-1}$. With slightly abuse of notation in the detailed proof, We introduce  egin{equation}\mathcal{G}_t = 
abla F(\wb_{t-1}) \quad 	ext{and} \quad \gb_t = 
abla f_t(\wb_{t-1}).\end{equation} We introduce the update $\ub_t \in \RR^d$, as well as the update without momentum $\Ub_t \in \RR^d$:  egin{equation} u_{t, i} =  rac{m_{t, i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t, i}}} \quad 	ext{and}\quad U_{t, i} =  rac{g_{t, i}+\delta_{t,i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t, i}}}. \end{equation} For any $k \in \NN$ with $k < t$, we define $	ilde{v}_{t, k} \in\RR^d$ by  egin{equation} 	ilde{v}_{t, k, i} =  eta_2^{k} v'_{t - k, i} + \esps{t - k}{\sum_{j=t- k + 1}^{t} eta_2^{t-j}(g_{j,i}+\delta_{j,i})^2}, \end{equation} i.e. the contribution from the $k$ last gradients are replaced by their expected value for know values of $f_1, \ldots, f_{t - k - 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce m', v', G_t, g_t, u_t, U_t and tilde v.

nodes.name: Smoothness descent inequality
nodes.statement: Using the smoothness of $F$, we have \begin{align*} &F(\wb_t) \leq F(\wb_{t-1}) - \eta_t \mathcal{G}_t^T \ub_t + \frac{\eta_t^2 L}{2}\norm{\ub_t}^2_2. \end{align*} The overall motivation of our proof is to find a lower bound for $\eta_t \mathcal{G}_t^T \ub_t$. \begin{align} \mathcal{G}_t^T \ub_t=\sum_{i\in[d]}\mathcal{G}_{t, i}\frac{m_{t, i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t, i}}} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: L-smoothness gives F(w_t) <= F(w_{t-1}) - eta_t G^T u + eta_t^2 L/2 ||u||^2.

nodes.name: Split into terms A and B
nodes.statement: We can rewrite $\mathcal{G}_t^T \ub_t$ as: \begin{equation} \sum_{i\in[d]}\mathcal{G}_{t, i}\frac{m_{t, i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t, i}}}=\underbrace{(\sum_{i\in[d]}\mathcal{G}_{t, i}\frac{m_{t, i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t, i}}}-\sum_{i\in[d]}\mathcal{G}_{t, i}\frac{m'_{t, i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t, i}}})}_A+\underbrace{\sum_{i\in[d]}\mathcal{G}_{t, i}\frac{m'_{t, i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t, i}}}}_B \end{equation} Here, Term A represents the error component arising from the quantization of the momentum accumulators ($\mathbf{m}_t, \mathbf{v}_t$), while Term B represents the behavior of the update driven by an ideal accumulator.
nodes.statement_short: Separate the moment-quantization error A from the ideal term B.

nodes.name: Bound A_1
nodes.statement:
Now we can bound term A. We split A into two parts as before:  egin{equation} |A| \le \underbrace{\left|\sum_{i\in[d]}\mathcal{G}_{t, i} rac{m_{t, i} - m'_{t,i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t, i}}}ight|}_{A_1} + \underbrace{\left|\sum_{i\in[d]}\mathcal{G}_{t, i}\left( rac{m'_{t, i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t, i}}} -  rac{m'_{t, i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t, i}}}ight)ight|}_{A_2} \end{equation} The first term, $A_1$, which arises from the quantization noise on the first moment $\mb$, is bounded using Lemma~ef{app:lemma:discrete_error_bound} (with $q=q_M$) and Lemma~ef{app:lemma:refined_cauchy}:  egin{align} |A_1| &\le \sum_{i\in[d]}R rac{|m_{t, i}-m'_{t,i}|}{\sqrt{v_{t, i}}} 
onumber \ &\le R\sum_{i\in[d]} rac{\sum_{k=0}^t( eta_1^{t-k}((1+q_M)^{t-k}-1))|
abla_i f_k(\wb_{k-1}) + \delta_{k,i}|}{\sqrt{\sum_{k=0}^t eta_2^{t-k}(1-q_V)^{t-k}(
abla_i f_k(\wb_{k-1}) + \delta_{k,i})^2}} \le q_M \cdot dR \cdot C_q \end{align} where $C_q =  rac{\sqrt{r'(1+r')}}{(1+q_M)(1-r')^{3/2}}$ and $r' =  rac{ eta_1^2(1+q_M)^2}{ eta_2(1-q_V)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the first-moment quantization part via the discrete error and refined Cauchy lemmas.

nodes.name: Reduce A_2 to a case analysis
nodes.statement:
For the second term, $A_2$, we use the bound on the gradient $
orm{\mathcal{G}_t}_\infty \le R$ and apply Lemma~ef{app:lemma:moment_relation}, which requires a case analysis.  egin{align} 
onumber |A_2| &\le \sum_{i\in[d]}R|m'_{t,i}|\left| rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t,i}}}- rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}}ight| \ &\le \sum_{i\in[d]}R|m'_{t,i}| \max\left\{  rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}} -  rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}},  rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}} -  rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+UB_{t,i}}} ight\} \end{align} Let $g_{k,i} = 
abla_i f_k(\wb_{k-1}) + \delta_{k,i}$. We analyze the two terms inside the $\max$ for a single coordinate $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound A_2 through the moment-relation lemma's max of two endpoint gaps.

nodes.name: Case I: lower endpoint
nodes.statement:
extbf{Case I (Deviation from Lower Bound):} Following the approximation in the provided sketch, we have  egin{align} 
onumber |m'_{t,i}| \left(  rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}} -  rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}} ight) 
onumber &=|m'_{t,i}|\left(  rac{v'_{t,i}-LB_{t,i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}(\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}+\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}})} ight)\ 
onumber &=  rac{|m'_{t,i}|}{\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}}  rac{v'_{t,i} - LB_{t,i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}(\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}+\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}})} \ 
onumber &\le  rac{|m'_{t,i}|}{\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}}  rac{v'_{t,i} - LB_{t,i}}{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}\ &\hspace*{-2cm} =  rac{\sum_{k=0}^{t}  eta_1^{t-k}|g_{k,i}+\delta_{k,i}|}{\sqrt{\epsilon+\sum_{k=0}^{t} ( eta_2(1-q_V))^{t-k} (g_{k,i}+\delta_{k,i})^2}} \cdot  rac{\sum_{k=0}^{t} ( eta_2^{t-k} - ( eta_2(1-q_V))^{t-k}) (g_{k,i}+\delta_{k,i})^2}{\epsilon+\sum_{k=0}^{t}  eta_2^{t-k} (g_{k,i}+\delta_{k,i})^2} \end{align} The first fraction is bounded by Lemma~ef{app:lemma:cauchy}: $ rac{\sum_{k=0}^{t} eta_1^k |a_{t-k,i}|}{\sqrt{\epsilon+\sum_{k=0}^{t}( eta_2(1-q_V))^k a_{t-k,i}}} \le  rac{1}{\sqrt{1- eta_1^2/( eta_2(1-q_V))}}$. The second fraction is a ratio of weighted sums $ rac{\sum_{k=0}^{t} ( eta_2^k - ( eta_2(1-q_V))^k) a_{t-k,i}}{\epsilon+\sum_{k=0}^{t}  eta_2^k a_{t-k,i}}$. This ratio is bounded by the maximum ratio of its coefficients:  egin{equation*} \max_{k \in \{0,\dots,t\}}  rac{ eta_2^k - ( eta_2(1-q_V))^k}{ eta_2^k} = \max_{k \in \{0,\dots,t\}} (1 - (1-q_V)^k) = 1-(1-q_V)^{t}. \end{equation*} Combining these bounds, the term for Case I is bounded by $ rac{1}{\sqrt{1- eta_1^2/( eta_2(1-q_V))}}(1-(1-q_V)^t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the lower-endpoint gap by 1/sqrt(1-beta1^2/(beta2(1-q_V))) (1-(1-q_V)^t).

nodes.name: Case II: upper endpoint
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case II (Deviation from Upper Bound):} Similarly, we bound the second term: \begin{align*} |m'_{t,i}| \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+UB_{t,i}}} \right) &\le \frac{|m'_{t,i}|}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}} \frac{UB_{t,i} - v'_{t,i}}{\epsilon+UB_{t,i}} \end{align*} Applying Lemma~\ref{app:lemma:cauchy} and the maximum ratio: \begin{equation*} \le \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \beta_1^2/\beta_2}} \cdot \left( 1 - (1+q_V)^{-t} \right) \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the upper-endpoint gap similarly.

nodes.name: Bound on A
nodes.statement: Comparing the bounds from the two cases, the bound from Case I is larger since $1-(1-q_V)^t > 1-(1+q_V)^{-t}$ and the denominator term $\sqrt{1 - \beta_1^2/(\beta_2(1-q_V))}$ is smaller than $\sqrt{1 - \beta_1^2/\beta_2}$. Therefore, taking the maximum and summing over $d$ dimensions: \begin{align} |A_2| \le \sum_{i\in[d]} R \frac{1-(1-q_V)^t}{\sqrt{1-\frac{\beta_1^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}}} = \frac{dR(1-(1-q_V)^t)}{\sqrt{1-\frac{\beta_1^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}}} \end{align} Combining the bounds for $|A_1|$ and $|A_2|$, we can get the bound for term A: \begin{equation} |A| \le |A_1| + |A_2| \le q_M \cdot dR \cdot C_q + \frac{dR(1-(1-q_V)^t)}{\sqrt{1-\frac{\beta_1^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}}} \triangleq Q(t) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Case I dominates; combine with A_1 to get |A| <= Q(t).

nodes.name: Split B into C and D
nodes.statement: Now we move on to bound Term B. Let us now focus on bounding Term B from \eqref{eq:fenli}. By expanding the definition of the first moment estimate $m'_{t, i}$, we can decompose Term B into two parts, which we will call Term C and Term D: \begin{align} \sum_{i \in [d]}\mathcal{G}_{t, i}\frac{m'_{t, i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t, i}}} &= \sum_{i \in [d]} \mathcal{G}_{t, i} \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \beta_1^k \frac{g_{t-k, i}+\delta_{t-k,i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t, i}}} \\ &= \underbrace{\sum_{i \in [d]} \sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\beta_1^k \mathcal{G}_{t-k, i} \frac{g_{t - k, i}+\delta_{t-k,i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+{v'_{t, i}}}}}_C + \underbrace{\sum_{i \in [d]} \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \beta_1^k \left(\mathcal{G}_{t, i} - \mathcal{G}_{t -k, i}\right) \frac{g_{t - k, i}+\delta_{t-k,i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t, i}}}}_D. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Expand m' to decompose B into the main term C and drift term D.

nodes.name: Bound D
nodes.statement: The magnitude of Term D, which captures the error from gradient drift, is bounded by Lemma \ref{lemma:bound_on_D}: \begin{align} |D| \leq \frac{\eta_t^2 L^2 \sqrt{1 - \beta_1}}{4 (1+q_G)R}\left( \sum_{l=1}^{t-1}\norm{\ub_{t-l}}_2^2\sum_{k=l}^{t - 1}\beta_1^k \sqrt{k} \right) +\frac{(1+q_G)R}{\sqrt{1 - \beta_1}} \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \left(\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_2}\right)^k \sqrt{k+1}\norm{\Ub_{t-k}}_2^2. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Term D lemma.

nodes.name: Lower bound C
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Term C lemma.

nodes.name: Lower bound on G^T u
nodes.statement: Injecting \eqref{app:eq:descent_proof:almost_there_main} ,\eqref{eq:d_bound_final_rearranged_main}and \eqref{eq:B_term_decomposition_main} into \eqref{eq:fenli} . We get the final lower bound for $\mathcal{G}_t^T \ub_t$: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\esp{\sum_{i\in[d]}\mathcal{G}_{t, i}\frac{m_{t, i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t, i}}}} \geq \frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{i\in[d]} \sum_{k=0}^{t - 1} \beta_1^k \esp{ \frac{\mathcal{G}_{t - k, i}^2}{\sqrt{\epsilon + \tilde{v}_{t, k + 1, i}}}}\right)-Q(t)-d\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\beta_1^kM_{t-k} \\ &\qquad - \frac{\eta_t^2 L^2}{4 (1+q_G)R}\sqrt{1 - \beta_1}\left( \sum_{l=1}^{t-1}\norm{\ub_{t-l}}_2^2\sum_{k=l}^{t - 1}\beta_1^k \sqrt{k} \right) - \frac{3 (1+q_G)R}{\sqrt{1 - \beta_1}} \left(\sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \left(\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_2}\right)^k \sqrt{k+1}\norm{\Ub_{t-k}}_2^2\right). \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Combine the A, C, D bounds into a lower bound on E[G^T u].

nodes.name: Plug into descent inequality
nodes.statement_short: Insert the lower bound into the smoothness inequality.

nodes.name: Bound tilde v
nodes.statement_short: Bound sqrt(eps + tilde v) by (1+q_G)R Omega_t.

nodes.name: Sum over iterations
nodes.statement_short: Telescope over t to get the inequality with terms tilde A, B, C, D, E_Q, M.

nodes.name: Rewrite tilde A
nodes.statement_short: Change index to express tilde A as weighted sum of gradient norms.

nodes.name: Random iterate tau
nodes.statement: To establish our convergence guarantee, we analyze the expected gradient norm at a randomly selected iteration $\tau$, drawn from the set $\{0, \ldots, T-1\}$. The selection is not uniform but is instead weighted to properly account for the influence of the momentum term over the iterations. The probability of selecting a specific iteration $t$ is defined as: \begin{align} \forall t \in \{0, \ldots, T-1\}, \quad \mathbb{P}(\tau = t) \propto 1 - \beta_1^{T-t}. \end{align} We can notice that \begin{align} \sum_{j=0}^{T-1} (1 - \beta_1^{T - j}) = T - \beta_1 \frac{1 - \beta_1^{T}}{1 - \beta_1} \geq T - \frac{\beta_1}{1 - \beta_1}. \end{align} Introducing \begin{equation} \tilde{T} = T - \frac{\beta_1}{1 - \beta_1}, \end{equation} we then have \begin{align} \tilde{A} \geq \frac{\eta \tilde{T}}{2 (1+q_G)R}\esp{\norm{\nabla F(\wb_{\tau})}_2^2}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Choose tau with P(tau=t) proportional to 1-beta1^{T-t} and lower bound tilde A.

nodes.name: Bound tilde B
nodes.statement: Next looking at $\tilde{B}$, we apply Lemma~\ref{app:lemma:u}, \begin{align} \tilde{B} \leq B' \left(\ln\left(1 + \frac{((1+q_G)R)^2}{\epsilon(1-\beta_2(1-q_V))}\right) - T\ln(\beta_2(1-q_V))\right) \end{align} with \begin{gather} B'= \frac{d\eta_T^2 L}{2(1 - \beta_1(1+q_M))(1 - \frac{\beta_1(1+q_M)}{\beta_2(1-q_V)})}. \end{gather}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the sum-of-updates lemma.

nodes.name: Bound tilde C
nodes.statement_short: Use Lemma A.4 then the sum-of-updates lemma.

nodes.name: Bound tilde D
nodes.statement_short: Use Lemma A.3 then the sum-of-ratios lemma.

nodes.name: Rewrite E_Q
nodes.statement_short: Sum Q(t) over t in closed form.

nodes.name: Bound M
nodes.statement: Finally, we bound Term M using Lemma~\ref{lemma:bound_on_M}: \begin{align} M \le \frac{\eta_T d T}{\sqrt{\epsilon}(1-\beta_1)} \left( q_G R^2 + L q_W R \norm{\wb_0}_2 \right) + \frac{\eta_T^2 d^\frac{3}{2} L q_W R T^2}{2\sqrt{\epsilon}(1-\beta_1)\sqrt{1-\frac{\beta_1^2(1+q_M)^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}}}, \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Term M lemma.

nodes.name: Assemble the detailed bound
nodes.statement_short: Combine all bounds into the detailed bound on E||grad F(w_tau)||^2.

nodes.name: Simplified bound
nodes.statement_short: Use tilde T >= T/2 to obtain the simplified bound stated in the theorem.

nodes.name: Plan of the asymptotic analysis
nodes.statement: Theory~\ref{thm:QAdam} states that under a specific schedule for the hyperparameters and a gradual reduction in quantization error, Quantized Adam achieves the same convergence rate as its full-precision counterpart. We prove this by performing a detailed asymptotic analysis of each term in the main bound from Theorem~\ref{thm:QAdam} as the total number of iterations $T \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Analyze the asymptotic order of each term as T grows.

nodes.name: Six-term detailed bound
nodes.statement_short: Write the detailed bound as Terms 1-6 under the scaling assumptions.

nodes.name: Quantization error schedules
nodes.statement: \textbf{Quantization Error Schedules:} The quantization errors are annealed over time such that $q_G = \mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$, $q_M = \mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$, $q_W = \mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$, and $q_V = \mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$.

nodes.name: Adam hyperparameters
nodes.statement: \textbf{Adam Hyperparameters:} The learning rate and second-moment decay are set as $\eta = \Theta(T^{-1/2})$ and $1-\beta_2 = \Theta(1/T)$, while $\beta_1$ is treated as a constant.
nodes.statement_short: eta = Theta(T^{-1/2}), 1 - beta2 = Theta(1/T).

nodes.name: Asymptotic analysis outline
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Asymptotic Analysis of Bound Terms.} We now analyze the order of magnitude for each of the six terms.
nodes.statement_short: Analyze each of the six terms.

nodes.name: Term 1
nodes.statement: \textbf{Term 1 (Initial Condition Term):} This term is given by $T_1 = 2 (1+q_G)R \frac{F_0 - F_*}{\eta \tilde{T}}$. We analyze the components of its denominator. The effective number of iterations is $\tilde{T} = T - \frac{\beta_1}{1 - \beta_1} = \Theta(T)$. The learning rate scales as $\eta = \Theta(T^{-1/2})$. The denominator thus scales as $\eta\tilde{T} = \Theta(T^{-1/2})\Theta(T) = \Theta(T^{1/2})$. Since all other quantities are constants and $q_G \to 0$, the entire term scales as: \begin{align*} T_1 = \Theta\left( \frac{1}{\eta \tilde{T}} \right) = \Theta\left(\frac{1}{T^{1/2}}\right) = \Theta(T^{-1/2}). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Term 1 is Theta(T^{-1/2}).

nodes.name: Term 2
nodes.statement: \textbf{Term 2 (First Logarithmic Term):} This term is: \begin{align*} T_2 = \frac{12 d ((1+q_G)R)^2 \sqrt{1-\beta_1}}{\tilde{T}(1 - \beta_1 / \beta_2)^{3/2}\sqrt{1 - \beta_2}} \left(\ln\left(1 + \frac{((1+q_G)R)^2}{\epsilon ( 1- \beta_2)}\right) - T \ln(\beta_2)\right) \end{align*} The leading fraction's order is determined by its denominator, $\tilde{T}\sqrt{1 - \beta_2}$. With $\tilde{T} = \Theta(T)$ and $1 - \beta_2 = \Theta(1/T)$, we have $\sqrt{1 - \beta_2} = \Theta(T^{-1/2})$. Thus, the fraction scales as $\Theta(\frac{1}{T \cdot T^{-1/2}}) = \Theta(T^{-1/2})$. The term in the parenthesis scales as $\ln(1+\Theta(T)) - \Theta(1) = \Theta(\ln T)$. The overall order is: \begin{align*} T_2 = \Theta\left(\frac{1}{\tilde{T}\sqrt{1 - \beta_2}}\right) \cdot \Theta(\ln T) = \Theta\left(T^{-1/2}\right) \cdot \Theta(\ln T) = \Theta\left(\frac{\ln T}{\sqrt{T}}\right). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Term 2 is Theta(ln T / sqrt T).

nodes.name: Term 3
nodes.statement: \textbf{Term 3 (Second Logarithmic Term):} This term is $T_3 = \frac{E}{\tilde{T}}\left(\ln(...) - T\ln(...)\right)$. First, we determine the asymptotic order of $E$, which is defined as: $$E=\frac{d\eta L(1+q_G)R(1-\beta_1)^2}{(1 - \beta_1(1+q_M))(1 - \frac{\beta_1(1+q_M)}{\beta_2(1-q_V)})(1-\beta_2)}+\frac{2d\eta^2 L^2 \beta_1(1-\beta_1)}{(1 - \beta_1(1+q_M))(1 - \frac{\beta_1(1+q_M)}{\beta_2(1-q_V)})(1-\beta_2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.$$ For the first part of $E$, the numerator scales as $\eta=\Theta(T^{-1/2})$ and the denominator is dominated by $(1-\beta_2)=\Theta(T^{-1})$. This part is $\Theta(T^{-1/2}) / \Theta(T^{-1}) = \Theta(T^{1/2})$. For the second part, the numerator scales as $\eta^2=\Theta(T^{-1})$ and the denominator is dominated by $(1-\beta_2)^{3/2}=\Theta(T^{-3/2})$. This part is $\Theta(T^{-1}) / \Theta(T^{-3/2}) = \Theta(T^{1/2})$. Thus, $E = \Theta(T^{1/2})$. The logarithmic part scales as $\Theta(\ln T)$, so the entire term scales as: \begin{align*} T_3 = \Theta\left(\frac{E}{\tilde{T}}\right) \cdot \Theta(\ln T) = \Theta\left(\frac{T^{1/2}}{T}\right) \cdot \Theta(\ln T) = \Theta\left(\frac{\ln T}{\sqrt{T}}\right). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Term 3 is Theta(ln T / sqrt T).

nodes.name: Term 4
nodes.statement: \textbf{Term 4 (Moment Quantization Error):} We rewrite this term as: \begin{align} T_4 = \frac{2(1+q_G)dR^2T(1-\beta_1)}{\tilde{T}\sqrt{1-\beta_2}}Q, \end{align} where $Q= q_M \cdot \frac{\sqrt{r'(1+r')}}{(1+q_M)(1-r')^{3/2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\frac{\beta_1^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}}}-\frac{1}{T}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\frac{\beta_1^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}}} \left( \frac{1-q_V}{q_V}(1-(1-q_V)^T) \right)$. Our goal is to show that $T_4 = \mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$. First, the pre-factor has an asymptotic order of: \begin{align*} \frac{2(1+q_G)dR^2T(1-\beta_1)}{\tilde{T}\sqrt{1-\beta_2}} = \Theta\left(\frac{T}{T \cdot T^{-1/2}}\right) = \Theta(T^{1/2}). \end{align*} The core of the analysis thus lies in determining the order of $Q$. We can rewrite $Q$ by combining its second and third components: \begin{align*} Q = q_M \cdot \frac{\sqrt{r'(1+r')}}{(1+q_M)(1-r')^{3/2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\frac{\beta_1^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}}} \left[ 1 - \frac{1}{T} \left( \frac{1-q_V}{q_V}(1-(1-q_V)^T) \right) \right]. \end{align*} The first part of $Q$ is clearly $\mathcal{O}(q_M) = \mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$. The common factor in the second part, $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\dots}}$, converges to a constant as $T \to \infty$, so it is $\mathcal{O}(1)$. The analysis therefore simplifies to finding the order of the bracketed term. Let $x = q_V = \mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$. We perform a Taylor expansion on $(1-x)^T$: \begin{align*} (1-x)^T = 1 - Tx + \frac{T(T-1)}{2}x^2 + \mathcal{O}(T^3x^3). \end{align*} This allows us to analyze the term inside the bracket: \begin{align*} 1 - \frac{1}{T} \left( \frac{1-x}{x}(1-(1-x)^T) \right) &= 1 - \frac{1}{T} \frac{1-x}{x}\left(Tx - \frac{T(T-1)}{2}x^2 + \mathcal{O}(T^3x^3)\right) \\ &= 1 - \frac{1}{T} (1-x)\left(T - \frac{T(T-1)}{2}x + \mathcal{O}(T^3x^2)\right) \\ &= 1 - \frac{1}{T} \left(T - \frac{T(T-1)}{2}x - Tx + \mathcal{O}(T^3x^2)\right) \\ &= 1 - \left(1 - \frac{T(T+1)}{2T}x + \mathcal{O}(T^2x^2)\right) \\ &= \frac{T+1}{2}x - \mathcal{O}(T^2x^2). \end{align*} Substituting back $x = q_V = \mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$, the bracketed term has an order of: \begin{align*} \mathcal{O}(T \cdot q_V) = \mathcal{O}(T \cdot T^{-2}) = \mathcal{O}(T^{-1}). \end{align*} Therefore, the entire second component of $Q$ is $\mathcal{O}(1) \cdot \mathcal{O}(T^{-1}) = \mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$. Combining both components of $Q$, we find its overall order: \begin{align*} Q = \mathcal{O}(T^{-1}) + \mathcal{O}(T^{-1}) = \mathcal{O}(T^{-1}). \end{align*} Finally, we compute the order of Term 4 by combining the pre-factor and $Q$: \begin{align*} T_4 = \Theta(T^{1/2}) \cdot \mathcal{O}(T^{-1}) = \mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2}). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Taylor expansion of (1-q_V)^T shows Term 4 is O(T^{-1/2}).

nodes.name: Term 5
nodes.statement: \textbf{Term 5 (Initial W/G Quantization Error):} This term is: \begin{align*} T_5 = \frac{2(1+q_G) d T}{\tilde{T}\sqrt{\epsilon(1-\beta_2)}} \left( q_G R^3 + L q_W R^2 \norm{\vec(\Wb_0)}_2 \right) \end{align*} The leading fraction scales as $\frac{T}{\tilde{T}\sqrt{1-\beta_2}} = \frac{\Theta(T)}{\Theta(T)\Theta(T^{-1/2})} = \Theta(T^{1/2})$. The parenthesis scales with its dominant term $q_G=\mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$. The total order is: \begin{align*} T_5 = \Theta(T^{1/2}) \cdot \mathcal{O}(q_G + q_W) = \Theta(T^{1/2}) \cdot (\mathcal{O}(T^{-1}) + \mathcal{O}(T^{-2})) = \mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2}). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Term 5 is O(T^{-1/2}).

nodes.name: Term 6
nodes.statement: \textbf{Term 6 (Weight Growth Quantization Error):} This term is $T_6 = \frac{(1-\beta_1)d^\frac{3}{2} \eta L q_W(1+q_G)R^2 T^2}{\tilde{T}\sqrt{\epsilon}(1-\beta_2)\sqrt{1-\frac{\beta_1^2(1+q_M)^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}}}$. First, we analyze $\sqrt{\frac{1}{1-\frac{\beta_1^2(1+q_M)^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}}}$. As $T \to \infty$, the denominator converges to the constant $1-\beta_1^2$, so its contribution is $\mathcal{O}(1)$. The term's order is determined by the scaling of its other components: $\eta=\Theta(T^{-1/2})$, $q_W=\mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$, $\tilde{T}=\Theta(T)$, and $(1-\beta_2)=\Theta(T^{-1})$. The total order is: \begin{align*} T_6 = \Theta\left(\frac{\eta \cdot q_W \cdot T^2}{\tilde{T} \cdot (1-\beta_2)}\right) = \Theta\left(\frac{T^{-1/2} \cdot T^{-2} \cdot T^2}{T \cdot T^{-1}}\right) = \Theta(T^{-1/2}). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Term 6 is Theta(T^{-1/2}).

nodes.name: Rate for squared gradient norm
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Conclusion.} By comparing the asymptotic orders of all terms, we identify those that converge to zero at the slowest rate, as they will dominate the overall convergence bound. The orders are: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item Term 1, 4, 5, 6: $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ or $\Theta(T^{-1/2})$. \item Term 2, 3: $\Theta(T^{-1/2} \ln T)$. \end{itemize} The dominant terms are the second and third, which are of order $\Theta(T^{-1/2}\ln T)$. These terms form the bottleneck that determines the overall convergence rate. Thus, under the specified parameter schedule, the expected squared gradient norm converges to zero at the following rate: \begin{align*} \esp{\norm{\nabla F(\wb_{\tau})}_2^2} = \Theta\left(\frac{\ln T}{\sqrt{T}}\right) = \tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\right). \end{align*} This matches the known convergence rate for full-precision Adam.
nodes.statement_short: Terms 2 and 3 dominate: E||grad F||^2 = O~(1/sqrt T).

nodes.name: Recall Jensen's inequality
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we derive the convergence rate for the expected gradient norm, $\esp{\norm{\nabla F(\wb_{\tau})}_2}$, from the rate of its squared value. We use Jensen's inequality, which states that for a convex function $\phi$ and a random variable $X$, $\phi(\mathbb{E}[X]) \le \mathbb{E}[\phi(X)]$.
nodes.statement_short: Jensen's inequality relates E[X]^2 and E[X^2].

nodes.name: Rate for gradient norm
nodes.statement_short: Jensen with phi(x)=x^2 gives E||grad F|| = O~(T^{-1/4}).

nodes.name: Two parts
nodes.statement: The proof consists of two parts.
nodes.statement_short: The proof has two parts.

nodes.name: Part 1: bounds on v
nodes.statement:
extbf{Part 1: Bounding $v_{t,i}$} The update rule for the second moment estimate is $v_{t, i} =  eta_2 (v_{t-1, i} + 	heta_{t-1,i}) + (
abla_i f_t(\wb_{t-1}) + \delta_{t,i})^2$. The quantization noise is assumed to be a relative error, bounded by $|	heta_{t-1,i}| \le q_V|v_{t-1,i}|$. This implies that $(1-q_V)v_{t-1,i} \le v_{t-1,i} + 	heta_{t-1,i} \le (1+q_V)v_{t-1,i}$. Applying this to the update rule, we can establish the lower bound by recursively unrolling the inequality:  egin{align} v_{t, i} &\geq eta_2(1-q_V) v_{t-1, i} + (
abla_i f_t(\wb_{t-1}) + \delta_{t,i})^2 
onumber\ &\geq eta_2(1-q_V) \left[  eta_2(1-q_V)v_{t-2,i} + (
abla_i f_{t-1}(\wb_{t-2}) + \delta_{t-1,i})^2 ight] + (
abla_i f_t(\wb_{t-1}) + \delta_{t,i})^2 
onumber\ &= \dots 
onumber\ &=\sum_{k=0}^t eta_2^{t-k}(1-q_V)^{t-k}(
abla_i f_k(\wb_{k-1}) + \delta_{k,i})^2 \end{align} Similarly, we can establish the upper bound:  egin{align} v_{t, i} &\le eta_2(1+q_V) v_{t-1, i} + (
abla_i f_t(\wb_{t-1}) + \delta_{t,i})^2 
onumber\ &=\sum_{k=0}^t eta_2^{t-k}(1+q_V)^{t-k}(
abla_i f_k(\wb_{k-1}) + \delta_{k,i})^2 \end{align} This completes the proof of the first statement in the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Unroll the second-moment recursion with factors beta2(1 -/+ q_V).

nodes.name: Part 2: inverse square root gap
nodes.statement: \textbf{Part 2: Bounding the difference of the inverse square roots} Let $v'_{t,i}$ be the idealized second moment estimate, updated without the quantization noise $\theta$. Its explicit form is: \begin{align} v'_{t,i} = \sum_{k=0}^t\beta_2^{t-k}(\nabla_i f_k(\wb_{k-1}) + \delta_{k,i})^2 \end{align} From Part 1, we know that $v_{t,i}$ is in the interval $[LB_{t,i}, UB_{t,i}]$, where $LB_{t,i}$ and $UB_{t,i}$ are the bounds established. Now, we compare $v'_{t,i}$ with these bounds. Since $0 < \beta_2 < 1$ and we assume $0 < q_V < 1$, we have $\beta_2(1-q_V) < \beta_2 < \beta_2(1+q_V)$. This implies a term-by-term inequality, leading to: \begin{align} LB_{t,i} < v'_{t,i} < UB_{t,i} \end{align} Consider the function $f(y) = 1/\sqrt{\epsilon+y}$ for $y \ge 0$. This function is monotonically decreasing and convex. The value $v_{t,i}$ lies in the interval $[LB_{t,i}, UB_{t,i}]$, and $v'_{t,i}$ is a point within this interval. The maximum absolute difference $|f(v_{t,i}) - f(v'_{t,i})|$ must occur when $v_{t,i}$ is at one of the endpoints of the interval. Therefore, we can bound the difference as: \begin{align} \left|\frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t,i}}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}}\right| &\le \max\left\{ \left|\frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}}\right|, \left|\frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+UB_{t,i}}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}}\right| \right\} \end{align} Since $LB_{t,i} < v'_{t,i} < UB_{t,i}$ and the function is decreasing, we have $1/\sqrt{\epsilon+UB_{t,i}} < 1/\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}} < 1/\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}$. We can therefore remove the absolute value signs: \begin{align} \left|\frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t,i}}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}}\right| &\le \max\left\{ \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+LB_{t,i}}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+UB_{t,i}}} \right\} \end{align} This completes the proof of the second statement.
nodes.statement_short: v' lies in [LB, UB]; monotonicity of 1/sqrt(eps+y) bounds the gap by endpoint gaps.

nodes.name: Error recurrence
nodes.statement: First, define the error as \( e_t = a_t - b_t \). Subtracting the two system equations yields the error recurrence relation: \begin{align} e_{t} = ke_{t-1} + kc_{t-1} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Define e_t = a_t - b_t and derive its recurrence.

nodes.name: Solve recurrence
nodes.statement: The explicit solution to this recurrence is \( e_{t} = k^{t}e_{0} + \sum_{j=0}^{t-1}k^{t-j}c_{j} \). Under the zero initial condition \( a_0 = b_0 = 0 \), this simplifies to: \begin{align} e_{t} = \sum_{j=0}^{t-1}k^{t-j}c_{j} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Unroll e_t as a weighted sum of perturbations.

nodes.name: Apply relative bound
nodes.statement: Taking the absolute value and applying the given condition \( |c_j| \le q|a_j| \), we have: \begin{align} |e_{t}| \le \sum_{j=0}^{t-1}k^{t-j}|c_{j}| \le q\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}k^{t-j}|a_{j}| \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound |e_t| by q times weighted |a_j|.

nodes.name: Bound the states
nodes.statement: Since \( a_0=0 \), the sum starts from \( j=1 \). The state \( |a_j| \) can be bounded from its own recurrence \( |a_{t}| \le k(1+q)|a_{t-1}| + |d_t| \), which for \( a_0=0 \) unrolls to: \begin{align} |a_{j}|\le\sum_{i=1}^{j}(k(1+q))^{j-i}|d_{i}| \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound |a_j| via its own recurrence.

nodes.name: Double sum
nodes.statement: Substituting the bound for \( |a_j| \) into the inequality for \( |e_t| \) gives a double summation: \begin{align} |e_{t}|\le q\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}k^{t-j}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{j}(k(1+q))^{j-i}|d_{i}|\right) \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute into the bound on |e_t|.

nodes.name: Swap sums
nodes.statement: By swapping the order of summation and evaluating the inner geometric series, we obtain the final result: \begin{align} |a_{t}-b_{t}| \le \sum_{j=1}^{t-1}\left[(k(1+q))^{t-j}-k^{t-j}\right]|d_{j}| \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the inner geometric series to conclude.

nodes.name: Numerator and denominator
nodes.statement: Let the numerator be \(N_t = \sum_{k=0}^{t} a^k |g_k|\) and the denominator be \(D_t = \sqrt{\sum_{k=0}^{t} b^k g_k^2}\). We rewrite the numerator as: \begin{align} N_t = \sum_{k=0}^{t} \left( \frac{a^k}{\sqrt{b^k}} \right) \cdot \left( \sqrt{b^k} |g_k| \right) \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Name N_t, D_t and factor the numerator.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz
nodes.statement: Applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to these finite sums, we get: \begin{align} N_t^2 &\le \left( \sum_{k=0}^{t} \left( \frac{a^k}{\sqrt{b^k}} \right)^2 \right) \cdot \left( \sum_{k=0}^{t} \left( \sqrt{b^k} |g_k| \right)^2 \right) \nonumber\\ &= \left( \sum_{k=0}^{t} \frac{a^{2k}}{b^k} \right) \cdot \left( \sum_{k=0}^{t} b^k g_k^2 \right) \nonumber\\ &= \left( \sum_{k=0}^{t} \left(\frac{a^2}{b}\right)^k \right) \cdot D_t^2 \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound N_t^2 by a geometric sum times D_t^2.

nodes.name: Geometric series bound
nodes.statement: The first term is a finite geometric series. Since the condition \(a^2 < b\) implies that the ratio \(r = a^2/b\) is positive and less than 1, all terms in the series are positive. Therefore, the finite sum is always less than or equal to the sum of the infinite series: \begin{align} \sum_{k=0}^{t} \left(\frac{a^2}{b}\right)^k \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{a^2}{b}\right)^k = \frac{1}{1 - a^2/b} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the finite geometric series by the infinite one.

nodes.name: Substitute and take roots
nodes.statement: Substituting this upper bound back into the inequality for \(N_t^2\), we have: \begin{align} N_t^2 \le \left( \frac{1}{1 - a^2/b} \right) \cdot D_t^2 \end{align} Taking the square root of both sides gives: \begin{align} N_t \le \sqrt{\frac{1}{1 - a^2/b}} \cdot D_t \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Get N_t <= sqrt(1/(1-a^2/b)) D_t.

nodes.name: Divide
nodes.statement: Finally, dividing by \(D_t\) yields the desired result for any finite \(t\): \begin{align} \frac{N_t}{D_t} = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{t} a^k |g_k|}{\sqrt{\sum_{k=0}^{t} b^k g_k^2}} \le \sqrt{\frac{1}{1 - a^2/b}} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Divide by D_t.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz
nodes.statement: Following the proof of Lemma~\ref{app:lemma:cauchy}, we apply the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to get: \begin{align} \left(\sum_{k=0}^{t} A_k |g_k|\right)^2 \le \left( \sum_{k=0}^{t} \frac{A_k^2}{B_k} \right) \cdot \left( \sum_{k=0}^{t} B_k g_k^2 \right). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz as in the previous lemma.

nodes.name: Express A_k^2/B_k
nodes.statement: This implies that the ratio is bounded by the square root of the first term on the right-hand side. We now focus on bounding the term $\sum_{k=0}^{t} \frac{A_k^2}{B_k}$. First, we express the ratio $\frac{A_k^2}{B_k}$ as: \begin{align} \frac{A_k^2}{B_k} &= \frac{(\beta_1^k((1+q_M)^k - 1))^2}{(\beta_2(1-q_V))^k} \nonumber \\ &= \left(\frac{\beta_1^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}\right)^k ((1+q_M)^k-1)^2. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to bounding sum A_k^2/B_k.

nodes.name: Mean value theorem
nodes.statement: To bound the term $((1+q_M)^k-1)^2$, we first establish an inequality for $(1+q_M)^k-1$ using the Mean Value Theorem. Let $f(x) = x^k$. For $q_M > 0$, by the Mean Value Theorem, there exists a $c \in (1, 1+q_M)$ such that: \begin{align} \frac{f(1+q_M) - f(1)}{(1+q_M)-1} = f'(c) \implies (1+q_M)^k - 1 = q_M \cdot (k c^{k-1}). \end{align} Since $c < 1+q_M$, and for $k \ge 1$, we have $c^{k-1} \le (1+q_M)^{k-1}$. This leads to the inequality: \begin{align} (1+q_M)^k - 1 \le k \cdot q_M \cdot (1+q_M)^{k-1}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: MVT gives (1+q_M)^k - 1 <= k q_M (1+q_M)^{k-1}.

nodes.name: Square
nodes.statement: Squaring both sides of \eqref{eq:mvt_inequality_lemma4} gives: \begin{align} ((1+q_M)^k-1)^2 &\le k^2 q_M^2 (1+q_M)^{2(k-1)} \nonumber \\ &= \frac{k^2 q_M^2}{(1+q_M)^2} (1+q_M)^{2k}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Square the MVT inequality.

nodes.name: Bound A_k^2/B_k
nodes.statement: Substituting this back into \eqref{eq:ak_bk_ratio_lemma4}, and using the definition $r' = \frac{\beta_1^2(1+q_M)^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}$, we get: \begin{align} \frac{A_k^2}{B_k} &\le \left(\frac{\beta_1^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}\right)^k \frac{k^2 q_M^2}{(1+q_M)^2} (1+q_M)^{2k} \nonumber \\ &= \frac{q_M^2}{(1+q_M)^2} k^2 \left(\frac{\beta_1^2(1+q_M)^2}{\beta_2(1-q_V)}\right)^k \nonumber \\ &= \frac{q_M^2}{(1+q_M)^2} k^2 (r')^k. \end{align}

nodes.name: Closed form of sum k^2 x^k
nodes.statement: Now we sum this term. The condition $r' < 1$ ensures the convergence of the infinite series. We first derive the closed-form expression for $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k^2 x^k$ for $|x|<1$. We start with the geometric series: \begin{align} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} x^k = \frac{1}{1-x}. \end{align} Differentiating with respect to $x$ and multiplying by $x$ gives: \begin{align} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k x^k = x \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right) = \frac{x}{(1-x)^2}. \end{align} Differentiating one more time and multiplying by $x$ yields: \begin{align} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k^2 x^k = x \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x}{(1-x)^2}\right) = x \frac{1(1-x)^2 - x(2(1-x)(-1))}{(1-x)^4} = \frac{x(1+x)}{(1-x)^3}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the geometric series twice.

nodes.name: Sum the bound
nodes.statement_short: Sum over k using the closed form.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Finally, taking the square root of \eqref{eq:sum_bound_final_lemma4} and substituting it back into the result from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality \eqref{eq:cauchy_applied_lemma4} gives the desired bound: \begin{align} \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{t} A_k |g_k|}{\sqrt{\sum_{k=0}^{t} B_k g_k^2}} \le \sqrt{\sum_{k=0}^{t} \frac{A_k^2}{B_k}} \le \sqrt{\frac{q_M^2}{(1+q_M)^2} \frac{r'(1+r')}{(1-r')^3}} = q_M \cdot \frac{\sqrt{r'(1+r')}}{(1+q_M)(1-r')^{3/2}}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Take square roots and combine with Cauchy-Schwarz.

nodes.name: Single component
nodes.statement:
We first bound the infinity norm of a single quantized gradient vector $
abla^Q f(\cdot)$. For any component $i \in [d]$, we have:  egin{align} \left| 
abla_i^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) ight| &= \left| 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) + \left(
abla_i^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) - 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j})ight) ight| 
onumber \ &\le \left| 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) ight| + \left| 
abla_i^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) - 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) ight| 
onumber \ &\le \left| 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) ight| + q_G \left| 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) ight| 
onumber \ &= (1+q_G) \left| 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma_{t,j}) ight|. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Each quantized component is at most (1+q_G) times the exact one.

nodes.name: Infinity norm of one gradient
nodes.statement_short: Take the max over components and use the gradient bound.

nodes.name: Average over batch
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality over the batch average.

nodes.name: Decompose the bias
nodes.statement:
We start from the decomposition of the conditional expectation of $\delta_{t,i}$, which we derived previously:  egin{align} 
onumber \espt{\delta_{t,i}}&= \mathbb{E}_{\gamma} \left[ 
abla_i^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma) - 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma) ight]+\mathbb{E}_{\gamma} \left[ 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma) - 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}; \gamma) ight]\ &= \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\gamma} \left[ 
abla_i^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma) - 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma) ight]}_{	ext{Term I: Gradient Quantization Bias}} + \underbrace{\left(
abla_i F(\wb_{t-1}^Q) - 
abla_i F(\wb_{t-1})ight)}_{	ext{Term II: Weight Quantization Bias}} \end{align} Using the triangle inequality, we can bound the magnitude as:  egin{align} |\espt{\delta_{t,i}}| \le |	ext{Term I}| + |	ext{Term II}|. \end{align} We bound each term separately.
nodes.statement_short: Split into gradient-quantization and weight-quantization biases.

nodes.name: Bounding Term I
nodes.statement:
extbf{Bounding Term I:} This term is the expected bias from the (potentially biased) gradient quantization. We first apply Jensen's inequality for absolute values, i.e., $|\mathbb{E}[X]| \le \mathbb{E}[|X|]$:  egin{align} |	ext{Term I}| &= \left|\mathbb{E}_{\gamma} \left[ 
abla_i^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma) - 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma) ight]ight| 
onumber \ &\le \mathbb{E}_{\gamma} \left[ \left|
abla_i^Q f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma) - 
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma)ight| ight]. \end{align} By the relative error model for gradient quantization (Assumption ef{assump:qe} with factor $q_G$):  egin{align} |	ext{Term I}| \le \mathbb{E}_{\gamma} \left[ q_G \left|
abla_i f(\wb_{t-1}^Q; \gamma)ight| ight] \le q_G R. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Jensen and the relative error give |Term I| <= q_G R.

nodes.name: Bounding Term II
nodes.statement:
extbf{Bounding Term II:} This term represents the bias from weight quantization. Using the L-smoothness of $F$ (Assumption ef{assump:smooth}) and the relative error for weights (Assumption ef{assump:qe}):  egin{align} |	ext{Term II}| = |
abla_i F(\wb_{t-1}^Q) - 
abla_i F(\wb_{t-1})| \le 
orm{
abla F(\wb_{t-1}^Q) - 
abla F(\wb_{t-1})}_2 \le L q_W 
orm{\wb_{t-1}}_2. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: L-smoothness and weight relative error give |Term II| <= L q_W ||w||.

nodes.name: Combining the Bounds
nodes.statement: \textbf{Combining the Bounds:} Summing the bounds for Term I and Term II, we arrive at the final result: \begin{align} |\espt{\delta_{t,i}}| \le |\text{Term I}| + |\text{Term II}| \le q_G R + L q_W \norm{\wb_{t-1}}_2. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Sum the two bounds.

nodes.name: Recall D and Young's inequality
nodes.statement: We start with the definition of Term D: $$D = \sum_{i \in [d]} \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \beta_1^k \left(\mathcal{G}_{t, i} - \mathcal{G}_{t -k, i}\right) \frac{g_{t - k, i}+\delta_{t-k,i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t, i}}}$$ To tackle this, we employ the weighted Young's inequality, which states that for any $\lambda > 0$, \begin{equation} xy \leq \frac{\lambda}{2}x^2 + \frac{1}{2\lambda}y^2 \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Recall the definition of D and the weighted Young's inequality.
nodes.section: A.9 Proof of Lemma lemma:bound_on_D (Bound on Term D)

nodes.name: Apply Young's inequality
nodes.statement: We apply this inequality to each product within the summation for Term D, setting \begin{equation*} x = |{\mathcal{G}_{t, i} - \mathcal{G}_{t -k, i}}|, \quad y = \frac{|{g_{t -k, i}+\delta_{t-k,i}}|}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v'_{t,i}}}, \quad \text{and} \quad \lambda = \frac{\sqrt{1 - \beta_1}}{2 (1+q_G)R \sqrt{k + 1}}. \end{equation*} This application gives us an initial bound on the magnitude of D: \begin{align} |D| &\leq \sum_{i \in [d]} \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \beta_1^k \left( \frac{\sqrt{1 - \beta_1}}{4 (1+q_G)R \sqrt{k + 1}}\left(\mathcal{G}_{t, i} - \mathcal{G}_{t -k, i}\right)^2 + \frac{(1+q_G)R\sqrt{k+1}}{\sqrt{1-\beta_1}}\frac{(g_{t -k, i}+\delta_{t-k,i})^2}{\epsilon + v'_{t, i}} \right). \end{align} To simplify this expression further, we must establish bounds for two of its key components.
nodes.statement_short: Choose lambda to split each product into two squares.
nodes.section: A.9 Proof of Lemma lemma:bound_on_D (Bound on Term D)

nodes.name: Denominator bound
nodes.statement: First, we can find a lower bound for the denominator term. For any coordinate $i \in [d]$, the recursive definition of $v'_{t,i}$ implies that $\epsilon + v'_{t, i} \geq \epsilon + \beta_2^{k} v'_{t -k, i} \geq \beta_2^{k} (\epsilon + v'_{t-k, i})$. This allows us to bound the fraction as: \begin{equation} \frac{(g_{t - k, i}+\delta_{t-k,i})^2}{\epsilon + v'_{t,i}} \leq \frac{1}{\beta_2^k}U_{t -k, i}^2. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: eps + v'_t >= beta2^k (eps + v'_{t-k}).
nodes.section: A.9 Proof of Lemma lemma:bound_on_D (Bound on Term D)

nodes.name: Gradient drift bound
nodes.statement_short: L-smoothness and Jensen bound ||G_t - G_{t-k}||^2.
nodes.section: A.9 Proof of Lemma lemma:bound_on_D (Bound on Term D)

nodes.name: Combine and rearrange
nodes.statement_short: Substitute both bounds and rearrange the summation.
nodes.section: A.9 Proof of Lemma lemma:bound_on_D (Bound on Term D)

nodes.name: Main term
nodes.statement: We study the main term of the summation in C, i.e. for $i \in [d]$ and $k < t$: \begin{align} \esp{\mathcal{G}_{t -k, i} \frac{g_{t-k,i}+\delta_{t-k,i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t, i}}}} = \esp{\nabla_i F(\wb_{t - k -1})\frac{\nabla_i f_{t -k}(\wb_{t - k - 1})+\delta_{t-k,i}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v_{t, i}}}}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Focus on a single (i,k) term of C.
nodes.section: A.10 Proof of Lemma lemma:bound_on_C (Lower Bound on Term C)

nodes.name: Notation s and r
nodes.statement: We will further drop indices in the rest of the proof, noting $\mathcal{G} = \mathcal{G}_{t - k, i}$, $g = g_{t -k ,i }$, $\delta=\delta_{t-k,i}$,$\tilde{v} = \tilde{v}_{t, k + 1, i}$ and $v = v'_{t, i}$. Finally, let us note \begin{equation} s^2 = \sum_{j=t- k}^{t}\beta_2^{t-j}(g_{j,i}+\delta_{j,i})^2 \qquad \text{and}\qquad r^2 = \esps{t - k - 1}{s^2}. \end{equation} In particular we have $\tilde{v} - v = r^2 - s^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Drop indices and define s^2 and its conditional expectation r^2.
nodes.section: A.10 Proof of Lemma lemma:bound_on_C (Lower Bound on Term C)

nodes.name: Rewrite with tilde v
nodes.statement:
With our new notations, we can rewrite~\eqref{app:eq:left_main_term_lemmaC} as  egin{align} 
onumber \esp{\mathcal{G}  rac{g+\delta}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v}}} &= \esp{\mathcal{G}  rac{g+\delta}{\sqrt{\epsilon+	ilde{v}}} + \mathcal{G}(g+\delta) \left( rac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v}} -  rac1{\sqrt{\epsilon+	ilde{v}}}ight)} \ 
onumber &= \esp{\esps{t -k - 1}{\mathcal{G}  rac{g+\delta}{\sqrt{\epsilon+	ilde{v}}}} + \mathcal{G} (g+\delta)  rac{r^2 - s^2}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v}\sqrt{\epsilon+	ilde{v}}(\sqrt{\epsilon+v} + \sqrt{\epsilon+	ilde{v}})}}\ 
onumber &= \esp{ rac{\mathcal{G}^2}{\sqrt{\epsilon+	ilde{v}}}} +\esp{ rac{\mathcal{G}\esps{t-k-1}{\delta}}{\sqrt{\epsilon+	ilde{v}}}}+\esp{\underbrace{\mathcal{G} (g+\delta)  rac{r^2 - s^2}{\sqrt{\epsilon+v}\sqrt{\epsilon+	ilde{v}}(\sqrt{\epsilon+v} + \sqrt{\epsilon+	ilde{v}})}}_{E}}\ &\geq \esp{ rac{\mathcal{G}^2}{\sqrt{\epsilon+	ilde{v}}}}- rac{q_GR^2+Lq_WR
orm{\wb_{t-k-1}}_2}{\sqrt{\epsilon}} +\esp{E}. \end{align} The inequality uses Lemma ef{lemma:delta_bound_biased_expected} and the bound for $
